speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subsubtopic: QUESTION OF RECOGNITION OF ASSOCIATION OF TECHNICAL EMPLOYEES-BOARD OF CONCILIATION
speechtext:
On May 5 the hon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) asked certain questions in regard to the association of technical employees and their relations with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have the answer to those questions, furnished by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which I will read:
The Association of Technical Employees advised the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on January 16, 1941, that the members of the engineering division of the CBC in Toronto had authorized them to apply for a collective agreement on their behalf. In this letter the following statement was contained ". .	. with recognition of this association previously established by the board of governors . . .". In a letter dated August 21, 1940, the general manager said, in a communication addressed to the chairman of the radio committee of the A.T.E. ... "I write now to tell you that the governors have accepted my recommendation about the attitude of the CBC to the A.T.E. There was, of course, no question of 'recognition'. What I recommended was the kind of cordial and effective cooperation which you and I discussed last week."
The letter of 16 January, 1941, was signed by Philip Dawes (not a member of the CBC staff) as national secretary of the A.T.E. In this letter it was suggested that the general manager of the CBC and Mr. J. A. Murphy of the corporation's Toronto engineering staff should have a talk about preliminary questions.

The general manager wrote to Mr. Murphy on February 6 and explained to him that any proposals he had to make must be referred to the board of governors both as to procedure and as to objective. The written proposals were received from the A.T.E. on February 20, 1941.
The proposed agreement was submitted to the Department of Justice and they were asked whether in their opinion "it is a fit and suitable contract for the corporation to sign."
The Department of Justice gave their opinion on April 17 stating "Your corporation is, in many respects, in the position of a department of the government and I would not think that the board of governors or the general manager would have the authority to enter into such an agreement which would restrict the authority of the corporation to act as freely as the government itself in all matters relating to its employees."
Under date of April 17, 1941, advice was received from the Assistant Deputy Minister of Labour that an application dated April 7, 1941, had been received by the Minister of Labour for the establishment of ". . .a board of conciliation and investigation to deal with a dispute between the CBC and its engineers, announcers, and producers being members of the Association of Technical Employees."
The corporation's answer to the assistant deputy minister was dated April 22. It was pointed out that the Department of Justice had given the opinion that the CBC was not authorized to enter into any agreement with the union as such. However, it was stated that the CBC was making every reasonable effort to allow its employees to express themselves through their appointed representatives and to negotiate as employees with the corporation regarding salaries and working conditions generally. It was further stated that the CBC was anxious to facilitate the establishment of staff councils throughout the entire service in order that both employees and the corporation would be in a position to have adequate means of discussing mutual problems.

I know of no general demand for such a committee; but I think it is the policy of the government to have such a committee at frequent intervals, to examine the report of the corporation and look into its affairs generally. speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for a very few minutes for the purpose of making a statement which I feel it my duty to make to-day.
I was absent from the house yesterday afternoon, attending a meeting of the war committee of the cabinet, and did not hear the speech made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond). I have seen a copy of that speech to-day, with deep regret. Still, the hon. member has merely repeated some of the things he said in this house when he opposed the participation of Canada in the war. The hon. member will permit me to say that he does not represent to-day, as he did not represent then, the sentiment of the province of Quebec. On two memorable occasions that province has spoken unequivocally and has rejected views similar to those expressed by my hon. friend. The voice of Quebec also has been heard on many

2652	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
occasions through the speeches of her leaders and the success with which all war service efforts have met when appeals were made.
I am particularly sorry that 'the hon. member spoke as he did, because of the false statements which appeared recently in certain publications, which are the work of ignorant and mischievous people. The words of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie will help the nefarious work of the enemies of Quebec. I would have expected the hon. member to modify his views in the light of events which have occurred since the outbreak of the war. Surely he should know, like all leaders of world opinion both spiritual and temporal, that to-day the very fate of civilization is at stake and no one has the right to be neutral. This he denied yesterday.
In his speech on September 9, 1939, when he opposed our participation in the war, the hon. member used the following words, which appear in Hansard, second session 1939, at page 63:
Why should we not adopt a policy which would keep us out of conflicts, as in the case of Belgium, Holland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Switzerland, Finland and so forth?
Then he continued:
But the difference between them and ourselves is that they are not seeking instruction in London, they are governed by their own interests.
Practically every one of the neutral countries mentioned by my hon. friend has been crushed, and has endured and is enduring innumerable and terrible sufferings. It is Herr Hitler who has brutally and barbarously answered the argument of my hon. friend; yet he still seems to stick to his policy of neutrality. I ask the hon. gentleman where else in the world would a citizen of a nation at war, a member of a legislative body, make a speech such as he made yesterday and be protected by the free institutions which are the glory and pride of a British parliament.
Fortunately this morning I saw an editorial which was published yesterday in a newspaper of Quebec City, L'Action Catholique, which certainly is not a political newspaper. I am going to read an extract from that editorial, which is in French, and I commend it to my hon. friend. The editorial has to do with a United States publication, Life magazine, and certain things which it said last week:
Here is the translation:
Stupid as it may be, Life's action affords us all a lesson: the lesson of carefulness and discretion. Life has evidently lied. But if we do not possess our Lindberghs, it is nevertheless unquestionable that we do not all have the

same understanding of the situation. As in every warring nation, some elements are found here who are not as much "in the war" as the rest.
Attacks like that of Life should make us more careful. A single word dropped in the press, from the speaker's platform, in social circles or even in private conversation, is enough, when a paper or a magazine uses it in a dishonest or blundering manner, to put us in a false position in the eyes of the world.
If there are some to whom has not yet been brought home the gravity of the hour for the world, for America, for Canada and for the French-Canadian people, we beseech them to do a little thinking. In times of danger, levity takes on a criminal character.
Since we are being spied upon by some who do not hesitate to distort our utterances, let us hold back every word whose meaning, misrepresented by a malicious whim, could make us seem to be what we are not. Even with the best intentions towards one's own people, the lack of a discipline based upon carefulness, wisdom and a good understanding of realities, can be prejudicial. Never has it been as necessary as it is to-day to keep watch on one's tongue.
My hon. friend has referred to two matters in connection with which I agree with him, but I am afraid his whole speech will be one of the arguments I shall have to face when I oppose the advocates of those policies which I will not accept. Instead of helping, he is doing great harm. Is that what he wants?
I intend, Mr. Speaker, in a very short time to broadcast some words to my own province, but meanwhile I desire to repudiate the words and opinions of the hon. member. My task and the task of my colleagues will be made, possibly, more difficult. His attitude will encourage the few ill-inspired individuals who are taking a most deplorable stand in the present situation. But we will do our duty and carry on the work necessary to the achievement of the purpose to which we have devoted ourselves. And I may assure hon. members that we will maintain in our province the fine unity of purpose and the spirit of harmony which has permitted Canada to do a great work since the opening of hostilities.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a deep sense of responsibility, after listening to the stirring words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that I now claim the privilege of addressing hon. members who are representatives of the Canadian nation at war. May I add, sir, that when I was preparing my speech the one to which the minister has referred was not in print. Coming from the western prairies, from one of the largest constituencies in

The Budget-Mr. Dechene
Canada, I say to the minister that the views he has expressed so eloquently to the house are held throughout that part of Canada. There are about 25,000 electors in my constituency, of whom about 5,000 are of French-Canadian origin; the others are drawn from almost every race under the sun. There are Canadian-born citizens from other provinces, thousands bom in the United States, and large numbers from almost every country in Europe. I am sure I speak for the great majority of my constituents when I say to the Minister of Justice that there is only one sentiment and only one voice in that great northland, and it supports to the full the war effort of Canada. It is with pride that I express in the house these sentiments on behalf of my constituents.
If the words hero, heroic and heroism had not already formed part of the English tongue we would at this time have had to coin them and write them into the lexicons of our language to describe the magnificent stand taken by the British, which was so ably and stirringly described yesterday by the Prime Minister of Australia. He referred to the conditions affecting the common people, the men and women of Great Britain, who for many months have been going through a terrific ordeal. They have shown marvellous courage and fortitude.
Those of us who have reached my age unfortunately are unable to offer service in one of the forces. Those of us who suffered from the depression are not in a position to help greatly with the financial situation. But there is one thing I can give and, if it is worth anything, I give it willingly. I have asked the privilege of taking the floor so that I might give my words, my voice, so that I might lend it to my country in this great crisis, to bring good cheer, to help in this time in carrying on our war effort, to show to everybody the necessity of meeting generously the taxation imposed by the budget now under debate. That voice, if it is worth anything, I offer to my government and my country. After prorogation I intend to give every minute of my time to help in this manner, because, unfortunately, it is the only way in which I am able to serve.
On Tuesday evening the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) addressed the house. I remember that part of Alberta when only the river was there, before the town had yet been built. This district has become one of the most prosperous parts of Alberta. I crossed that stream before there was even a ferry; I had to ford it many years before the mem-14873-168}
ber for Red Deer was born. It amazes me to hear him speak of pioneering in the west and refer to the terrible treatment of the pioneers by this government. With reference to the hon. member's use of the word "pioneer", it is with pride that I say that fifty years ago last fall I had the honour, as a little boy, to become a settler of the great province of Alberta, I ask him, as a friend of Alberta, to leave this word alone in the future. This noble word can be applied to the builders of western Canada, the Olivers, the Ross's, the Davis's, the La-combes, the Princes, and the Chevignys. These men and others like them were the architects of the western plains. These men were the type of men referred to by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Gregory); they have done much to contribute to the welfare of this country.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the debt that they created?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member will just listen, I will reply to him in the words of the hon. member for The Battlefords. He has occupied more of the time of this house than I have. I have been very patient, listening for hours to some of the things which he has peddled-pardon the expression-to this house. All I ask is that I be permitted to use my own time, having given the promise that I shall be as brief as possible.
I do not suppose he cares about it, but speaking on behalf of the people I represent I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon the presentation of his budget. It was not an easy task, because one who imposes taxes is never popular. It all depends upon whose ox is being gored. Every hon. member is willing to tax the other hon. member; every fellow is willing to let George pay the taxes, but no one seems to want to have taxes that affect his own pocket. The minister did a splendid piece of work, if he did nothing else than indicate to the members of this house and the people of the country the tremendous war effort which has been undertaken. The people who will have to meet these tax bills, the people who will have to subscribe to a loan and produce $2,500,000,000 this fall, will realize that Canada is carrying on generously and bravely, as she should; they will know that Canada has undertaken her full share in this struggle for existence.
As I address the house this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I realize that the beast of prey is snapping his teeth at the jugular vein of Great Britain in the battle of the Atlantic. You and I who have read the press of late, who have listened to Mr. Churchill, who have
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

listened to President Roosevelt and Secretary Stimson, who have listened to our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); those of us who have 'been able to understand the things which cannot be told but which have been implied, realize the magnitude of this battle upon which will depend the fate of the one nation which stood in the way of the conqueror, unprepared as she was, and gave the free men of the world an opportunity to prepare themselves, as we did in Canada, in Australia, in south Africa, and as the great republic to the south is doing at this moment.
I have referred to the leaders of democracy, and I have mentioned some great names, names that will live forever in the history of this world wherever freedom is respected. In the years and centuries to come, whenever men gather together to discuss the effect of this crucial period upon world history, in the schools of all lands where freedom and liberty may still exist, the names of Churchill, Roosevelt and Mackenzie King will live forever. No less a person than Wendell Willkie, the great American leader, has named these three as the great leaders of democracy to-day. Had it not been for the attitude adopted by certain people in Canada I would have hesitated to take up more of the time of this house.
Last fall, as the representative of Athabaska, I attempted to tell this house what Canada owed to the Prime Minister for the services which he has rendered to humanity. Strange as it may seem, I received a letter from a man who belongs to the same group as the hon. gentleman who just interrupted me. If you please, this man wanted to know what I meant by praising the Prime Minister. I received a letter from another man who wanted to know what I hoped to get from, it. What a narrow view! Is there anyone here who hopes to get anything out of this war except liberty? This thought was ably expressed yesterday by the Prime Minister of Australia. As he said, what does it matter if we are to be bankrupt, so long as we are able to live in a world where freedom and liberty exist? But this man went on to say that if I were a little rough and tough with the Prime Minister I might get more for Athabaska. What can a man hope to get for Athabaska at this stage of the game?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was he a member of parliament?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, and he never will be. But he was a supporter of the man who ran against me in the last election and lost his deposit.

A feeling exists throughout the world- unfortunately more strongly in Canada; why I am unable to explain-that seems to make people hate to recognize the things which are done on their behalf by those who give their lives in the service of their country. We can get applause from any audience by simply mentioning the name of Franklin Roosevelt. Hon. members will pound their desks at the mention of Churchill. But what happens when you mention the Prime Minister of Canada?
The Prime Minister of Canada did more than any other man to bring the two great democracies together. He was able to do this because of his great knowledge of conditions in the United States, because of his appreciation of what the sentiment was in that country, because of his personal friendship with the President of the United States. That made it possible to bring about the understanding which now exists between the two countries. All one has to do is to mention reciprocity, to mention Ogdensburg, to mention Hyde Park, to realize the momentous steps which have been taken in the history of this country and in the history of Great Britain and of the world. During the later years of his life the Prime Minister has seen erected these monuments to his ability, to his understanding and to his services to Canada and the world.
An amendment to the budget has been moved by our friends of the Social Credit party-or is it the New Democracy? I never have been able to find out. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, if we were to pay our soldiers, our sailors and our airmen with that celebrated fountain-pen money of the prophet Aberhart in Alberta! What a wonderful way of expressing our thanks to the gallant men who are risking their lives for us! I will ask hon. members of the Social Credit party to take a message back to the big prophet in Alberta.

I will say to my vociferous friend, who follows the man who sabotaged and torpedoed the Sirois conference, that he might well ask Premier Aberhart to withdraw from the income taxation field as suggested by the Minister of Finance. Premier Aberhart torpedoed the Sirois conference not for the same reason, that actuated British Columbia or Ontario, because, after all, Ontario stood to lose something by the adoption of the Sirois recommendations, but Alberta had everything to gain. I say to this man who sabotaged the conference that he ought to do something to help win this war. He should immediately accept the offer of the Minister of Finance and withdraw from the field of income taxation. The offer of the Minister of Finance was a generous one. He offered to pay over to Alberta, if the province vacated the income tax field-and I say that it is the duty of the province to do so-a lump sum equivalent to the amount of income tax collected by Alberta in 1940. We fear that Premier Aberhart will not accept this offer because very few of the small people with whom he deals are liable to income tax. If this offer of the Minister of Finance is not accepted, our merchants and business men in Alberta may be compelled to pay double income taxation. I say as a member from Alberta that it is the duty of the Aberhart government to follow the example of the other provincial governments, accept the offer of the Minister of Finance and withdraw from the income tax field.
We are spending almost two and a half billion dollars on the war, almost one-half of which is to finance British purchases in Canada. Let the province of Alberta do its share and assume the burden of the three-cent tax on gasoline and not allow it to be passed on to the consumer. That would be but a small thing for Alberta to do. Last

The Budget-Mr. Dechene
year Alberta had the largest budget of expenditure in the history of the province, and I do not include in that $25,000,000, in round figures-$24,758,000, to be exacb-the $3,500,000 of just debts which Alberta refused to pay to the municipalities of Ontario and to other provinces which had invested their savings in what they considered to be gilt-edged securities of the province of Alberta. And that budget, providing for the greatest expenditure in the history of Alberta, was brought down by a government that was going to reduce taxation! So I say that we have a right to expect Alberta to do its share, in view of its huge expenditure, and in view of the fact that Premier Aberhart thought the province could afford to increase his own salary at the last session, as was done.
I do not know whether this tax of three cents on gasoline applies to trucks and tractors used on farms or only to automobiles, but that does not matter; it has been found necessary and it is everyone's duty to pay it. But what do we find in Alberta? They have done nothing but discourage the people.
My time is nearly up and I shall have to leave until another occasion, perhaps at some other session, some of the things I wanted to say. We shall come back here and there will be another opportunity for us to consider such questions as the resettlement of the vast northeastern part of Alberta and the Peace River district. There are many possibilities of settlement and development in that part of the country in connection with the timber industry, fisheries and so on, and when the time comes I shall submit plans for the consideration of my fellow members.
In this time of crisis we should be careful in safeguarding the right of everyone in this democracy to speak freely. It is a right that I enjoy and a right which my friends opposite, apparently, enjoy quite well.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's manners are poor and his arguments rotten. He does not understand the word "service. He does not know what it means to be a citizen of the country and to meet the demands of the times as the Prime Minister and his cabinet are doing to-day. T.he members of the ministry have no family life of their own;

The Budget-Mr. Homuth
twenty-four hours of the day every day of the week they are devoting themselves to the duties entrusted to them in the administration of the various departments of government.
Let me ask hon. gentlemen who are so fond of criticism to consider the fact that something like $1,000,000,000 was spent during the last twelve months, and that, in the expenditure of this vast sum of money, not a single dollar has been questioned. There has not been the slightest suspicion, not a shadow of doubt in regard to the spending of all this money. There may be errors in the spending of it. If there had not been some errors it would indeed be strange. I know that if any minister said that he had made no mistakes at all-well, if he is not married, then I say he will never get married, because no woman would love a man like that. The integrity and honesty of this government have never been called in question. Their record is a remarkable one, and I am proud to pay them that tribute.
When we go back to the country, I say to hon. members of all parties, let us impress upon our constituents the importance of service to-day. Some of us are too old to serve, but there is still something that we can do. There are many ways in which we can serve democracy. Democracy lives on sacrifice and service; it is the very life-blood of democracy. When the day comes that men and women are no longer found ready to serve their country, wherever they can, without remuneration, whether in civic life or in the provincial field or in this great assembly, then we shall not need to fight, because democracy will have ceased to exist. So long as there are men willing and anxious to give their time to their country, the best that is in them, their thoughts and talents, then there is hope for our democracy. The Liberal teaching is the democratic teaching in this regard, and that is that the man in his shack in the Peace River or in the Athabaska country is just as important to the welfare of the country as the greatest man in Canada.
Life is intricate, and democracy is one of the monuments of God. You cannot take away the smallest wheel in the machinery of democracy without injuring the whole mechanism; if you do, it will cease to operate. That is what I have said to the people. I have never suggested to them that they can get something for nothing, that they can be exempt from taxation, or that they can obtain relief without the country paying for it in some w'ay. I say to hon. gentlemen and to the people, in this hour of trial for Canada, let us carry on and give to our country the best that is in us, whether as school trustees, as
aldermen, as members of legislatures or as members of this parliament.
Whatever sacrifices we may have to make under the budget we should make gladly. We shall not pay as much as Ontario and Quebec, but we will do our part; we will do our share. And, Mr. Speaker, not only in spending the money. I say to the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie and anyone who heard him that courage, loyalty, is not the appanage-I think that is a good word-or the monopoly of any nation. In Canada, in Athabaska, every race stands willing to do its share. And they will do it nobly, knowing that when this war is over, as was so stirringly said yesterday in this chamber-and I want to repeat those words-we may have nothing left. But actually we shall have a great deal left. We shall have pride in ourselves, in our boys. If those of us who lived through the last war, as I did, and who live out this war, as we hope to do, cannot leave to our children any heritage of this world's goods, let us so act that we shall leave to them a heritage of glory and of duty well done.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): May I first extend my very deep sympathy to the loved ones of those who were lost in the terrible sea disaster last week. Such tragedies as this bring home to us only too clearly the terrible havoc of war. Perhaps they do more; when this war is brought home to us as these tragedies bring it home, it steels in us the determination to go on and on with the fight for freedom until those who are responsible for this struggle are driven to their knees and the terrible tragedy of war is brought to their own country.
Yesterday afternoon we were privileged to hear in this chamber an address which to my mind was one of the most inspirational ever delivered in this house or in this country, a speech that I felt would reecho in the hearts of every hon. member of this house and every man and woman who heard it or read it in the press. It was a call to arms. It was a call to every one of us to go on with the job that we have to do. It reminded us that in this job there can be no east and no west, no religious divisions, no distinctions of nationality. It was a call to every one of us to go on in a bigger and better way even than we have in the past.
Then shortly after that speech had been delivered, what happened? An hon. member of this house rose in his place and made a speech of which I am not going to read any part into the record, because I feel that once on Hansard is sufficient for any such speech as that. I am particularly pleased that the
The Budget-Mr. Homuth

Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) rose in the house to-day and repudiated that hon. member and his sentiments. I am glad he did it, because someone had to do it, and in that regard no one had a greater responsibility than the Minister of Justice. Had he not done it I would have felt that I had much more to say about that speech than I have said; and unfortunately when one does deal with a speech of the kind in this chamber at a time like this he might be inclined to use bitter words for which he might be sorry later. I feel that the sentiments expressed by that hon. member are his alone, that there are no other hon. members in this house who would think of standing here and expressing them. The hon. member said that we are fighting only because British interests are in danger. Everything that we hold dear, as the Prime Minister of Australia said yesterday and as has been said so often in this house, the future of our children, our church, everything we have, is at stake, and as the hon. member who just sat down (Mr. Dechene) has said, if, when this war is over, we have nothing of a material nature left to us we shall at least have our freedom and the chance of building a future under that freedom.
I rise to-day not particularly to criticize the budget. I endorse my leader's stand on the budget; I intend to vote for it. But there are a few matters with which I should like to deal, because I feel that if we are not careful we are going to build up in this country a regimentation that we shall not be able to get rid of when the war is over. What I am fearful of is the advising body, the men- who to my mind are formulating the policies of the government.
I followed closely the debate on agriculture. Listening to hon. members from various parts of this country who have discussed questions affecting agriculture and the dangers they say are going to beset the agriculturist in various parts of Canada, one is almost led to believe that the agricultural policy of the government is the brain wave, not of men who are engaged in agriculture, but of men who see a very serious problem before them and try to find what they think would be the easiest way out. It looks to me as though we are going to build up in western Canada mixed agriculture; western Canada is to be looked upon as the agricultural district of Canada, while the east must develop industrially. That to my mind will be the result of the policies brought down by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
The only way to develop a real national economy in Canada is to develop industries from one end of this country to the other. In Alberta and in Saskatchewan there are

vast stores of fuel of various kinds, fuel with which power can be developed cheaper than we can develop hydro-electric power in Ontario. There are places in the western provinces where industries can be and should be built up. What will that do? So often I have heard hon. members from western Canada questioning industry and industrialists and the policies that are necessary in this country to build up industries. They seem to feel that the industries of eastern Canada are more or less parasitic and are taking a great deal of wealth and life out of the west. Such statements as these, I believe, are often made because hon. members from districts where there are no industries do not really understand the problems of industry. Scatter the industries throughout the country; then you will bring home to the people in all constituencies some of the problems with which industry is faced, and at the same time you will develop for the farmers a local market, which is the best market they can have. Go through western Ontario, with its local industrial centres and local markets. The farmers in those districts have not suffered to anything like the extent that the farmers have suffered in districts where there are no industries. If we are to have regimentation, at least let us be careful in our planning. Sometimes when I look at the ministers sitting opposite I just imagine how they long for the days of the past when they fought so bitterly against any planned economy for Canada. Now they have come to it, and I repeat that I am afraid we are not going to get away from it so easily later on.
Another feature of the budget which I think should be considered very carefully is the danger of the curtailment of certain industries in this country. I was amazed the other day to learn of the large number who are still unemployed in Canada. The minister, by levying taxes, is trying to curtail the manufacture of certain commodities which he classes as luxuries. I quite agree that if it came to the question whether a soldier should have a uniform or a civilian a new suit of clothes, the uniform should be provided. I quite agree that if it should come to the question of producing either a washing machine or part of an aeroplane, the aeroplane part should be made. But SO1 long as we have a large number of unemployed, and so long as we have the industrial capacity to produce these things, we should do everything possible to encourage that production, thus taking people off the relief rolls and getting them into the earning class. They would then be in a position to help produce; they would help create wealth; they would help pay taxes, and it would be beneficial all round. Perhaps there was a time when

The Budget-Mr. Homuth
washing machines, electrical appliances and even bathrooms were considered to a certain extent luxuries; to-day they are necessities. Our whole system of living has changed, and I think in these budgets we should be careful not to impose taxes which will lower the standard of living. Even with the war on surely we should do everything possible to maintain the standard of living, and when the war is over we should try to raise it beyond the level of to-day.
There is one matter, however, which I feel certainly deserves the serious consideration of the minister. I believe he should amend those provisions of the budget which are going to impose such tremendous taxes upon the low income groups of this country. The minister has stated that our national income has increased by a billion and a half dollars, or more; I think those were his figures. That may be true, but a statement of this kind gives people a false picture of the situation. When they read it they are inclined to believe that our national income has increased because of the fact that individual incomes have increased, while as a matter of fact the increase in our national income is largely due to the circumstance that tens of thousands of people are back at work now who for years were unemployed. While, therefore, it is true that our national income has increased, the individual income is not very much larger.
In this budget we are levying much higher taxes on all our people. The thousands of people who were unemployed for years are endeavouring to-day to pay off many of their old bills; to do the little things for their families and their homes that they have been unable to do for a long time; to purchase what they really need, but the very heavy taxes proposed by this budget will not permit them to do these things. The taxes now proposed will take away a great deal of the money they need for their family expenses. The average working man in Canada is getting little enough to provide any luxuries for himself and his family, and I feel that some of these taxes are most unfair to him, particularly when you consider what he has gone through in the last eight or ten years. We ask him to save by buying war savings certificates. We ask him to pay a national defence tax. We ask him to contribute as much as he can to the war services funds. The working men have responded. In my district a real effort was made to have the employees of every industry contribute one hundred per cent, and the effort was very successful. But what is the picture? In one industry the employees have so much taken off their pay for a scheme of health insurance maintained in that plant; so much for contributions to the war services fund; so much
for war savings certificates; so much for the national defence tax, and in July there will be another deduction from their pay for unemployment insurance. The pay envelopes of these employees are invaded five times before they actually get into the hands of the workers.
I 'believe all this is the start of the spiral of inflation. Not long ago I wrote the Department of Labour asking for their figures on the family budget in the various provinces. We will have an opportunity to debate these matters when the labour estimates are under consideration, but these budgets provide only for the bare necessities of life. Under an order in council it is provided that wages must have a relation to the cost of living; that is, if the cost of living in Canada goes up, wages must go up also. Surely these taxes are part of the cost of living. Surely if we keep levying more and more taxes on our people they will demand higher wages.

Oh, quite so, but the worker is more or less forced to buy war savings certificates. It is being put up to him in such a way that he feels he must buy them. These things are all part of the cost of living; and as a result of our system of taxation we are going to help bring about inflation in this country. I do not know whether it is a bad thing; but I do know that we cannot go on levying more and more taxes upon the people without their getting something with which to pay them. They have to get the money with which to pay the taxes.
There is one tax in particular against which I wish to protest. I refer to the tax on theatre tickets. In this instance the government is levying a tax against something which all must admit is the poor man's pleasure. The records for last year-and these are government records-show that of all the patrons of motion picture theatres throughout Canada 77 per cent were patrons of theatres having an entrance fee of 25 cents or less. There are only about ten theatres in Canada which have an entrance fee of over 50 cents. The minister said yesterday that the government was going to defer collection of the tax so that arrangements could be made under which it could be passed on to the patrons of theatres. If the minister felt the theatres were making large sums of money and that he should have some of it, then there should have been some other system of taxation.
The Budget-Mr. Homulh

But the tax has been levied on the tickets, and payment is to be deferred so that it may be passed back to theatre patrons.
The man who walks into the Chateau Laurier and pays three dollars for his dinner pays no tax. The man who buys a five-dollar ticket for a symphony concert pays no tax. The man who pays a dollar and a half or a dollar to attend a hockey match pays no tax.

speechtext:
Under the new ruling the federal government will not be taxing these things I have mentioned. Why not? Why does it not levy a tax where the people can afford to pay it? I believe that if taxes were levied in the places I have mentioned the government would collect almost as much as it will by taxing the poor man's theatre ticket.
In the United Kingdom at the beginning of the war, when bombs were dropping, the government closed the motion picture theatres. Afterwards however they found they had to open them so as to keep up the morale of the people. People in the. United Kingdom were encouraged to attend the motion picture theatres. When an ordinary building is bombed and destroyed, rebuilding cannot take place without the government's consent; but when a moving picture theatre is destroyed, and there are no other theatres within easy reach, automatically the government issues a permit for the rebuilding of the theatre, because it wants the people to have places to which they can go for entertainment.
A man will stand at his machine all day; a farmer will work in the field from morning until night; but in the evening he wants to have some enjoyment, some pleasure. He cannot afford expensive pleasures, but the motion picture theatre offers him the relaxation he requires. At a cost of only 25 cents for himself, 25 cents for his wife and 15 cents for his child, a total of 65 cents, the small family can enjoy two hours of entertainment. Now we say to the labouring man, "Your theatre tickets are going to cost you more money." We know, too, that if the admission price figures out to an odd cent, that extra cent will be added to the price [Mr. Homuth.l
of the ticket, as it was added in connection with the tax on cigarette papers which became effective after the last budget.
These are some of the provisions of the budget which I feel should be withdrawn. We should do everything possible to encourage the worker and to keep up his morale. We are asking our factory workers to work long hours, seven days a week. All labour regulations in the various provinces have been cleared off the slate so far as war industries are concerned. Let us be careful as to how we handle the men on whom we depend so largely for the production of the things England needs. At the same time let us take the same interest in the mothers and the children at home, who are doing so much to help the men in their jobs at the factories. These are matters I hope the minister will take under advisement, and I hope that when the resolutions are under consideration he will recommend some changes.
I do not wish to delay the business of the house. Before taking my seat, however, may I add my support to what has been said by many hon. members from all parts of the house with regard to the taxation of soldiers' railway tickets. There is no reason why the government should not exempt soldiers' railway fares from taxation. In fact the government might very well pay soldiers' railway fares for the one or two long leaves they receive. I do not say that soldiers should receive week-end passes on the railways or anything of the kind, but I do suggest that at least in respect of the long leaves they should not have to pay railway fares.
Let me give a picture of the present situation. The Highland Light Infantry, from my county, is now stationed at Debert, Nova Scotia. It costs the men of that regiment $30 to travel from their camp to their homes in Galt, Ontario. Yet here in my hand I hold an advertisement, appearing in maritime newspapers, which sets out special rates for civilians, and states that one may travel from Halifax to Toronto or North Bay and return for $20. The ticket is good for six days. If such concessions can be granted to the civilian population,, surely we can do as much for the soldiers.
One of the officers sent me this clipping, with the comment that while the officers might be able to pay their fares, it was much more difficult for the privates in the ranks to do so. Part of their pay is sent home. He pointed out that on occasions when men have received word of serious illness at their homes and have obtained special leave, they have had to pass the hat to get enough money to buy a railway ticket. We dare not be coldblooded about these things. If the railways

The Budget-Mr. Hansell
can grant special rates to civilians, why can the government not say to them, "You must do the same thing for the soldiers who are fighting to protect your very interests".
As I said earlier, I am going to follow my leader and support the budget. I realize that we must pay and pay and pay. I realize that we must have money to fight this war and to destroy the thing which is threatening the peace of the world. But I say to the minister that there are many places where he could economize. As the watchdog of the treasury I do not think he could do better than appoint a committee, even a committee of this house, to consider these matters. The committee which has been set up to consider war expenditures is going to get nowhere, but a committee of this house could go a long way in advising the ministry as to the many ways in which economies could be effected, thus permitting money to be diverted into the channel in which it ought to go. The people of Canada are going to give the minister the money he wants, but the people of Canada are going to require the government to account for the way in which it is spent.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but I do not think the speech of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) should be allowed to pass without a reply being given to-day. I am not so much concerned with the criticism which is usually offered in connection with the Alberta government. We who have been in this movement for the past several years are used to that sort of criticism. We are not so much concerned when men rise up and call Social Crediters crack-pots or silly fools or any other expression which they might desire to use. We are not so much concerned when people remind us that we believe in a national dividend and that in the Alberta provincial election of 1935 that dividend was estimated at $25 a month. We are not so much concerned about those things, but when any hon. member from Alberta rises in his place in this house and declares that the premier of that province, that the government of that province or that the people of that province are disloyal to the British empire, then we protest most vigorously.
Yesterday we listened to the Prime Minister of Australia. I had the privilege of hearing that honourable gentleman at the Canadian club luncheon in the Chateau Laurier, and we all had the privilege of listening to him speak on the floor of this house. I think every individual who listened to him was inspired, inspired to a greater war effort, inspired to greater unity among the various
nations of the British commonwealth. His message was followed shortly by a message to this house by the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond). I do not intend to offer severe criticism of that speech, although I think the hon. member was all wrong in his attitude. To-day we heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) make a statement in defence of the government in reply to what the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Laprairie had said yesterday. But may I remind the Minister of Justice that the hon. member for Beauhamois-Laprairie is sitting in this house to-day because of the war-time election policy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I believe the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie was wrong, but I believe also that he has a sense of honour. He does not go out through his constituency one time and say one thing, and then come to this house and say something else. I have in my hand an editorial which was published in the Toronto Telegram after the last general election, and I should like to quote this comment:
There is no use pretending that the electors have given King a mandate for a more vigorous prosecution of the war. The reverse is the case. The King government was indicted on a charge of holding back and denying Britain loyal cooperation and the charge was backed up with abundant evidence.
I am not saying that. I read that simply as an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Telegram after the last general election. But that must have been the impression and the opinion of a vast number of people in Canada at that time. What was the stand of the Alberta government at the time? I would take hon. members back to before the declaration of war upon Germany by this country. I would take them back as far as September 5, 1939. I should like to read certain statements which were made by the premier of Alberta at that time, and then I shall ask people to judge whether the Alberta government is loyal to our war effort. As I sat here and heard the hon. member bring down such a tirade upon Alberta, I declared to myself that that was an insult to the men from Alberta who are in uniform.
What was the declaration of the premier of Alberta at that time? The premier gave a statement to the press, and later, on September 14, he gave, over the air, a message to the people of Alberta. I do not intend to read the entire message, but I should like to quote some excerpts from it. The premier said:
We were firmly convinced-
The past tense is used because there had been a meeting between the Social Credit members of parliament and the premier of
The Budget-Mr. Hamell

Alberta and his cabinet. The special war session had been called, and it was thought that perhaps Canada would be declaring war upon Germany. A meeting was called between the provincial government and our members of parliament, and we discussed the matter. We came to this house-I might say that the hon. member for Athabaska was not here at that time-and as a consequence of the meeting which had been held in Edmonton we dared to go further in proposing Canada's war effort than any other party in this house went at the time. I ask hon. members to refer to the speech made at that time by our house leader; I ask them to read it and see for themselves the stand we took. That stand was taken as a result of the meeting with the premier of Alberta. Let me read from his broadcast. Referring to that combined meeting he said:
We were firmly convinced that a great wastage of life and property can be prevented by throwing the full weight of our resources behind Britain and her allies at the very beginning of the conflict.
Further on in the broadcast he used these words:
I want to say in conclusion that the provincial government have every desire to give its civil servants the privilege of taking any part they wish in connection with this struggle and we assure them that we will guarantee their reinstatement in the civil service when they return. This will alsq include the safeguarding of their superannuation rights. . . .
May I say that the provincial government and the federal social credit members took the uncompromising stand that in the present conflict Canada should give the mother country the most effective support possible. This surely meant that Canada should take her place with Great Britain and the British empire and organize all her resources in order to perform her utmost in this conflict with a proper sense of responsibility and with a full realization of the grave issues that are at stake. Subsequent events have shown conclusively that this is the united attitude of the nation as a whole.
Further on, he said:
These were the definite proposals-
He had been citing a good many of the proposals in our platform.
These were the definite proposals submitted, but in addition to them there are other important matters which have arisen and which also need your careful attention. No one will question the fact that it is most essential that there shall be the closest possible cooperation between all provincial governments and the federal government at this time. That cooperation this government intends to give unstintingly. This means that we shall press into the service of the nation all the help we can give without reserve even though it be with those who have hitherto been our political opponents. I should like to emphasize that point.
The premier went on to mention to his radio audience some of the things which the

Alberta government had taken upon themselves to do to help the dominion government. Most of them are concerned with the matter of prices. There is, for instance, the appointment of an investigator to examine with regard to supplies, to ensure that there shall be no restriction of supplies, and so forth and so on. The premier continued:
We feel sure that in taking this firm stand we are not only helping the federal government in its difficult task but that we shall have the people of the province solidly behind us. We are in a terrific struggle. It is essentially vital that no misunderstanding should disrupt our complete and effective support of the British empire in removing from the world one of the greatest menaces to true democracy that has arisen in the last quarter century. Remember the exhortation of Abraham Lincoln on a similar occasion, "United we stand, divided we fall".
As I conclude with that quotation, may I say that if 'Canada is to listen to such tirades of abuse as the hon. member for Athabaska brought down this afternoon upon the heads of a certain section of the people of this country, we had better not send him across Canada, for he would tear this country apart from stem to stern. What we want in this country to-day is unity, and there are no people more anxious for unity in our war effort than the people of Alberta and the premier of that province.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As evidenced by his stand at the recent dominion-provincial conference.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Since my hon. friend the member for Calgary West has mentioned that matter, which was also mentioned by the hon. member for Athabaska, we have men in our group who are quite capable of entering into a discussion of the Sirois report. But that is another matter. The hon. member for Athabaska bravely said that he was willing to meet any man on the public platform. Well, we have met men before on the public platform and discussed the Sirois report, and we shall be glad to do so again at any time and place.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And with any other hon. member.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One cannot always discuss matters at the time they are brought to one's attention; but may I add this, that the day will come when premiers Hepburn, Patbullo, and Aberhart will be seen as the heroes of that conference, not the wreckers of it. There are some men who are not willing to hand over their economic liberty to a centralized financial dictatorship.
I wish to refer to the speech that was made in this house on May 1 by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). The hon.

The Budget-Mr. Hansell
member is a French-Canadian. He has never had very much use for social credit, but I did admire his attitude when he was speaking on May 1. I am going to quote his words, and I want the house to notice the difference between his attitude and that of the hon. member for Athabaska to-day. At page 2460 of Hansard the hon. member for Cochrane said:
We have seen the development of the Social Credit party and other progressive movements. If an easterner takes the trouble to study those developments thoroughly he will find there is a reason for such political and economic eruptions. We may describe as fallacious and dishonest such things as debt repudiation in the west, but I suggest we cannot throw them out as easily as that. We must look into them more thoroughly. We must study social credit and its cause in our political life, approaching it from the western viewpoint, the reason for its flourishing; and always remembering that it is the policy of one of our great western provinces. The same reasoning must be applied to debt repudiation and other political movements of the last thirty-five years.
I cannot always agree with the hon. member for Cochrane, but if his attitude as expressed in those words is the attitude of this house, there is a little hope of our getting together and understanding one another. But to have to sit and listen to such an exhibition as we had this afternoon from the hon. member for Athabaska could, I am certain, have only the opposite effect.
I shall conclude, Mr. Speaker, by reiterating -and I cannot do it too often'-that the government of Alberta and this group here are as loyal as anyone in Canada to the British empire and to Canada's war effort. May I add that in 1935, when this group was first elected to the House of Commons and before we ever came here, we issued to the press a statement of our policy with regard to foreign relations. That policy has been reiterated here over and over again-a policy of absolute loyalty to the British empire, a policy of national defence such as at that time this country did not know.
When	this government first brought
down an appropriation for national defence in 1937, I believe-that is when they began to wake up-a great number of people in the Liberal party voted against that appropriation. As I recall, an amendment was submitted that the appropriation for national defence for that year be reduced to $1. Men in this group voted against the amendment and for the appropriation, because we had, I think I can say, vision enough to see what the country was eventually coming to. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) reminds me that all our leaders did that very thing.
It ill behooves anyone to rise in his place in this house and indulge in such abuse as that indulged in by the hon. member for Athabaska with the intention of putting in the minds of the Canadian people the impression that the social credit philosophy is against the best interests of the British empire.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He does not know any better.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would remind hon. members of the statement made by the Right Hon. Mr. Menzies yesterday in an interview with the press in which he declared a financial policy very much akin to what this group had been advocating for the past number of years. If this government had adopted some of the principles we have been proposing in the last six years in this house, our war effort would be a long way ahead of what it is to-day.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Even if they had adopted their own.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. What did we discover in 1935? The Prime Minister went on the stump and declared that he would take up the cudgels against the money-powers. He was going to issue currency and credit in terms of public need.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So he did.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did some one say, "so he did?" For ten years there have been about one million people in the country on relief; at least there were until a few years ago. Was that not public need? Did we not have public need when the war broke out? What is the attitude of this government? What has it been right along? It is this: "We will do just as much as we have money to do it with." The social credit philospohy is the converse of that. The social credit philosophy says: "What do we need?" I know what happens when the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) wants to build a dozen ships. He goes to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and says, "How much money can you give me to build a dozen ships?" The Minister of Finance tells him. If some other minister wants something else he does the same thing. The social credit philosophy is the opposite of that. It says: "We need ships. Not, how much money have we, but how much steel have we? How much engineering skill have we? How much raw materials have we? Then we will make our financial resources fit our needs; we will make our financial system reflect the physical possibilities."
The Budget-Mr. Hansell

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is true
patriotism.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is true patriotism, as some one has said. I regret having to make this speech altogther extemporaneously, because I had no time to go to my office and pick up certain quotations which I wanted to use; but I recall that the Prime Minister was going to do battle with the money-power. That was in 1935. What happened? Some time after that, the government bought fifty-one per cent of the stock of the Bank of Canada. The quotation to which I wished to refer was one from the London Times of England. The Times declared that the financial world had nothing to fear from the Prime Minister's action in buying fifty-one per cent of the stock of the Bank of Canada. A year or so later, the Prime Minister came down with the announcement that he would purchase 100 per cent of the stock of the Bank of Canada. You should have heard the Liberal majority pounding the boards out of their desks, as though we were going to enter into a glorious millennial golden age. But the next day, or a couple of days after, a Liberal government was returned in Saskatchewan.
I would challenge the government to tell the house one thing. I would challenge the Minister of Finance to tell the house one thing. I would challenge them to tell the house whether or not the banking policy of the country has changed one little tiny bit since the government took control of the Bank of Canada. I would challenge them to tell me whether the policy of the Bank of Canada has changed one bit, whether the financial system of the country has changed one tiny bit since they took control of the Bank of Canada. I would suggest to hon. members that if they want to examine the records of the Bank of Canada to discover whether the policy has changed, they will be refused access to those secrets.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Bankers' secrets.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, as my hon. friend the member for Vegreville says, it is a bankers' secret. I placed on the order paper last session a question asking whether the minutes of the directorate of the Bank of Canada were available to the people's representatives, the members of this house. The answer I was given was an emphatic no. I told that to one gentleman in my constituency and he was alarmed. He said, "What! A government-owned bank and yet the people's representatives cannot read the minutes of the board of directors." I wanted these minutes only to discover whether there had been any change in the banking policy

of the country; that is all. But one cannot get access to these minutes. One thing that is guarded with jealous secrecy is Canada's financial policy, which is inherently linked with the financial .policy of every other country in the world; for let us remember that finance knows no such thing as national boundaries.
An hon. MEMBER; And no patriotism.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and finance knows no such thing as patriotism. Those leaders who bow down in humble obeisance to the present financial system are more careful to save the system than to save the empire.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Utterly false.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry if my speech this afternoon has been rather disjointed, but I do not think the hon. member for Athabaska should go unanswered. Let it never be said that the social credit forces of this country, or the government and the premier of Alberta are disloyal to Canada's war effort or to the British empire.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not need to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), because we did that when he sat down, but I should like to congratulate the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) upon their constructive criticism. I thought it was helpful.
In the word "budget" there is music for all those who prefer to pay taxes to losing the war. There is one thing about the budget that ought to please any hon. member,, namely, that the money which is collected from many sources and put into manufacturing for the war goes back again to the toiler.
I would also congratulate the government upon their care for the men and women at the bottom of the pyramid in the civil service. Fifty or sixty dollars a month does not seem very much, but the increase was certainly well received. I would also remind the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) that there are more boys and more girls who follow the same studies in school and start work in local offices and banks who get far less. The Minister of Labour would do well to look into the salaries that are paid to bank clerks; for I have known young men who worked in a bank for six years before they got sixty dollars a month. This is not right. His Honour the Speaker of this house leads us each day in the petition to the-

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor
Master Workman, "lead us not into temptation," but the bankers are not observing that precept. I think of our soldiers; they also have had an increase of twenty cents a day; and as I have listened to hon. members speaking about railway fares for soldiers I am sure my hon. friends would join me when I say that I would rather pay the tax on my pass or have my pass revoked altogether than have the soldiers obliged to pay a tax on their tickets. I was one of those who thought, and I still think, that a soldier away from home and serving faithfully for small pay should have a free fare.
A little while ago in Fort William we had a banquet to a returned soldier, a real man. I refer to Colonel Doctor McCartney, who organized the fourth field ambulance and has now returned home. He thrilled that big audience by saying there were no politics in promotions overseas. Doctor McCartney was well known for his stand in politics. I do not need to say he was not a Liberal, but even so, he had a great deal of common sense. There are other places besides overseas where there are no party politics in war work, and I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) for one of the latest appointments, when the former leader of his majesty's loyal opposition in this house was sent to Great Britain as Colonel R. J. Manion. I take this opportunity of expressing the thanks of those in Fort William who supported me and of those who did not. We think the government made a fine choice in that appointment and did a fine act for our country.
I think also of the service that our government has given to the men who toil, in the legislation passed not long ago that gives a man the right to belong to any union he chooses and makes it a criminal offence for anyone to be dismissed because he belongs to a union. We had a splendid example of how the government sees that its own policy is put into practice when in the city of Hamilton the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) took control of affairs. To-day anybody would be short-sighted if they did not see a new social order coming into being. At the beginning of the war there were many industrial concerns that refused to operate for a five per cent profit. What did the government do? I cannot give the number of industrial concerns taken over by the government, but hon. members know they were not a few, where the machinery was purchased and the
plant set up and controlled by the government. This shows the coming of the new social order referred to by the Prime Minister in his splendid speech. No matter what interpretation may be put upon it by some hon. members, it is going to be better than anything we have had before. This idea is supported by the splendid speech made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) at the close of last session.
The reason why I am speaking to-day is that I see an improvement, not in the war work but in the life of Canada. I should like to give one example. Within a short distance of Thunder Bay we have a splendid opportunity in the development of iron ore, as spoken of frequently by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). But what I wish to speak of particularly now is the socialization of the muskrat. I do so because it has meant a great deal to the finances of this government, and will mean more in the future.
In northern Manitoba there are nearly two million acres of territory broken up with rivers and small lakes which in days that are past was a great trapping ground. I am not now going into details of this vast scheme because I expect to do so later on when the estimates are up. It was found that the muskrats had practically disappeared from this vast district, although it contained all kinds of natural food for them. Our scientists tried to open up this territory for agriculture, but their attempt was a failure. After the professional men failed, however, a nonprofessional in the person of Tom Lamb, of Moose Lake, undertook an experiment. He found that food for the muskrats was there in abundance, and he wondered why the muskrats were not there. He gave consideration to fall trapping, too intensive trapping, rat spear, disease, epidemics, fur cycles and so on, but none of these seemed to satisfy him. Then he thought it might be because of lack of water, and conceived the idea that instead of the Saskatchewan and other rivers flowing through, leaving no water behind, he might erect dams and retain some water. This he did, and as a result 135,000 acres were selected, which are now in production after four years of water control, conservation and protection. Another area of about 160,000 acres is about to enter its third year. Splendid support was given by Hon. J. S. McDiarmid of Manitoba and the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). This district north of The Pas now stands out as one of the greatest examples of socialism in the fur trade.
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor

I should like to give hon. members figures to show the growth of this industry, in terms of rats:
Number of rats
Start (1935)	 500
First year (1936)	 4,000
Second year (1937)	 20,000
Third year (1938)	 65,000
Fourth year (1939)	 164,000
Fifth year (1940)	 377,000
The value of these rats has increased from $30,000 in 1937, $100,000 in 1938 and $250,000 in 1939 to more than $600,000 in 1940. These were the results obtained by this young man, employed by the Department of Indian Affairs, who does not take any credit to himself but who carried on this work partly in his spare time and partly during office hours. The second project is now in its third year, and the figures with regard to it are as follows:
Number Number of houses of rats
Start	(1938)	65	520End of first year... (1939)	719	5,750End of second year (1940)	5,047	40,376
I mention this matter, Mr. Speaker, in order to suggest that if the brains of this country were applied to the socialization of our war industries as this young man applied his brains to this project, we would have no unemployment in Canada. I wish also to express the hope that something will be done in connection with the iron ore and other minerals which we have in such vast quantities at the head of the lakes. All we need is some brilliant man to apply himself to that problem, with the support of the government, and we shall realize a tremendous national benefit.
Coming back to the question of the war, I should like to make another suggestion. I know we do not all agree on these matters; we are all made differently, but I am convinced that no industry and no human being can thrive while working seven days a week. The law of God and man says that a man requires one day's rest in seven; a worker will do more work in six days than he will do in seven, and at the same time he will be happier about it and there will be less discontent and less labour trouble. One question has been asked me many times in connection with our war effort, and perhaps I would not be speaking out of turn if I mentioned what that question is. I am asked, "How do we know that God is on our side?" I wonder how hon. members would answer it? My reply is something like this: It is not whether we know that God is on our side but whether we know we are on His side; and we know, by the way we think and act, whether 
or not we are on His side. To me the only thing that will count after we win this war will be a life that is surrendered to the Prince of Peace; and when we have that, we shall have a social order that will have no backfires. When I think of our country and our empire, I am heartened and encouraged. I used to read history a bit; and if I have not forgotten what I read, the reason for the fall of Chaldea, the fall of Persia, the fall of Rome and the fall of ancient Greece was not that the common people were corrupt, but that the leaders became corrupt and citizenship could be purchased for cash. I take courage when I think of our king and queen, than whom there have been none better on the throne of England, and when I think of the Prime Minister of Britain and the leaders in the commonwealth of nations. Yesterday in this house we had the great leader of a sister dominion; and I am sure many hon. members noticed, as I did, the reverent way in which that great man referred to the Supreme Being. Then, when I think of our own leaders, I know we are on the right side, that we are bound to win, because the devil is going to lose in this battle.
We shall have many heart-burnings before this war is over; no doubt we shall have many moments of doubt before the terms of this budget are fulfilled. Many questions will have to be answered, although personally I find it far easier to explain this budget than to meet its obligations. If, however, each of us is willing to do his part; if every man keeps himself right, then we shall be able to give leadership to our constituents.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think we all appreciate the magnitude and difficulty of the task that confronted the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in preparing the budget now before us. Taking the budget by and large, I would not be honest, either with the minister or with myself, if I did not say that in my opinion he accomplished a difficult job fairly well. I have, however, a few criticisms to offer. Most of what I am going to say has been dealt with by other speakers, and consequently I shall deal with each point very briefly.
My first criticism is directed against the increase in the national defence tax on the lower incomes. I protested against this tax last year, and pointed out to the best of my ability the undue burden which it placed upon people whose incomes were already too low to give them a decent standard of living. This year the minister has raised from $600 to $660 the amount of income exempted from the tax. But the increased exemptions are already more than offset by the increase in

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
the tax, and the increased cost of living over that of last year. Single persons in receipt of incomes of $660 and married persons with incomes of 31,200 are at the best of times getting just a mere subsistence. To the extent that those incomes are reduced by taxation, just to that extent is the subsistence reduced, and health and morale, and our war effort is retarded.
I know the minister might have imposed indirect taxes which would have raised as much or more revenue than will be raised by the increase in the national defence tax. I believe, however, that quite properly he preferred the more direct and harder method. For that I am grateful. But it does not make the tax on these people any lighter. To a great many people this tax means that they are going to be on reduced rations so long as the war lasts. I would suggest that if we are going to ration some of our people, it would be better to ration all of us. I, therefore, wish to associate myself with other hon. members, including the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), who have already protested against the increase in this tax. For purposes of the national defence tax there is no reason why the exempted incomes should not be the same as they are in respect of the ordinary income tax, namely, $750 for single persons and $1,500 for married persons.
I should like to say a few words with respect to death duties or inheritance taxes. This is a new departure for the federal government, and I wish to commend the Minister of Finance for it. While agreeing with the criticism of the leader of the opposition with regard to the application of the national defence tax to low incomes, I cannot agree with him in his strictures on the inheritance tax. I agree with the Minister of Finance that death duties provide an eminently fair form of taxation. Whatever reasons may exist for not making a capital levy on accumulated fortunes while the original owners are alive, that reason disappears when the owners die and the fortunes pass to others who took no part in their accumulation. The tax is to be graduated according to the size of the estate. The minister stated, for example, that there would be a tax of $8,500 on an unearned, inherited fortune of $100,000. In my opinion that is not excessive. Indeed, it is excessively mild when we compare it with a tax of $35 on the earned income of a person making $700 a year.
There is another modification in the income tax I should like to criticize. I refer to the reduction in the tax on the timber industry. In fact I would protest in the strongest possible terms against the proposed reduction
in this tax. It is not warranted. I do not know what the situation may be in other provinces, but I know that in British Columbia for years the lumber operators have carried on their business with the utmost disregard for any and every interest except their own. They operated the industry with the utmost abandon and criminal waste. The minister said the operators were becoming alarmed because of the rapid depletion of valuable timber limits. This is the first time it has come to my notice that lumber operators in British Columbia have ever given any consideration to the greatest asset of that province, except to get as much profit out of it at as little cost as possible. Log-cutting practices of British Columbia, as carried on by the lumber companies during the last twenty-five years, has been a major crime. The method of logging has been such that far more timber has been destroyed annually than has been produced. Logged-off areas were left in such a condition as to be a continuous fire hazard.
