The result has been that, of our British Columbia forests, at one time the finest in the world, more have been destroyed by fire than have been converted into timber.
Then, in addition to that, it was next to impossible to secure the cooperation of the operators in British Columbia for any measure of forest conservation. They may have been acting a little better during the last few years, but their record is exceedingly bad. What many British Columbia lumber operators, both past and present, should get, is not favourable consideration with regard to income tax but a term in the penitentiary.
I wish now to say a few words respecting the amendment moved for the Social Credit group by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). The amendment reads:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"This house regrets the failure of the government to establish effective control over the issue of credit by the chartered banks to the end that the amount by which the proceeds from reasonable taxation and sale of interest-free war savings certificates fails to meet government expenditures, may be met by funds from Bank of Canada, without fear of inflation.
This amendment divides itself into two parts, in the first of which it advocates government control of the issue of credit. We agree entirely with that, and could gladly support that part of the amendment.
The second part, however, seems to be obscure. It refers to the raising by funds from the Bank of Canada, of that amount of the revenue which cannot be raised by taxation and interest-free war savings certificates. I do not at the moment know what is meant
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

by "interest-free war savings certificates". I do not believe the government is issuing any such certificates at the present time. I know a certain type of war bond, non-interest bearing, is being issued by the government, but unfortunately they are not advertised. I am not sure that I understand the words "by funds from Bank of Canada." I do not know whether it is intended to raise additional revenue by the issue of currency, or whether it is to be done by some other means. If it is the intention to raise additional revenue by the issue of currency, we should keep in mind the fact that the amount to be issued will be enormous. I believe that my figures are correct and that the amount will range from a minimum of around $700,000,000, the expected deficit on Canada's account alone, to a maximum of $1,668,000,000, the combined deficit on Canadian and British accounts. In any event, one gathers from the amendment that the amount to be raised is large, because mention is made of the dangers of inflation. To guard against inflation the amendment proposes, "effective control over the issue of credit by the chartered banks." That is to prevent the money issued by the Bank of Canada from being made the basis of further credit by the chartered banks when it reaches them.
With regard to the necessity of there being effective control over the chartered banks, this group is in agreement with our Social Credit friends. In fact I think we are to some extent ahead of them because we have been advocating this for many years. It seems to me that the amendment admits that the government policy as operated through the Bank of Canada may be nullified by the action of the privately owned chartered banks, or because of lack of control over the chartered banks. I think we can also agree with that. We have advocated for years government ownership and control of Canada's financial system, to the end that the government, acting in the interests of the people as a *whole, should be in complete control of the country's [DOT]financial resources. Therefore, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas):
That all the words after "banks" in the third line of the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Further that in order to achieve a maximum and equitable war effort, the nationalization of the financial system and its use as an instrument of public policy are fundamental steps in the elimination of interest and the dangers of inflation."
We propose this subamendment because, while we agree with part of the main amende ment, other parts are not quite clear to us.

There is another matter with which I should like to deal and which is not mentioned in the budget. For the last two or three sessions I have had upon the order paper a resolution in connection with the matter of old age pensions, but because of the war situation no time has been given to a discussion of these resolutions. I was prepared to deal with this matter at length, but after listening to the capable manner in which it was dealt with by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) a few evenings ago, I shall confine my remarks . to merely mentioning the subject.
I am in receipt, almost daily, of letters from old people who find themselves in the most difficult circumstances because they are not able to get old age pensions on account of some provision in the regulations or because the amount of the pension is not sufficient for them to live on. I noticed in the Montreal Gazette of March 5 a report from the French federation of charities which pointed out that the increased tempo of production since the war began is placing more and more men and women in the "too-old-to-work class". This report states:
To the people who are out of the job category and still too young for old age pensions is now being added a new class of people unable to fend for themselves. They are men and women who emerged from the depression without work, without money reserves, and without relatives able to help them. Consequently, demands upon social organizations caring for such cases are heavier than ever, despite the expansion of employment as a whole.
The government should realize that, while industry has increased considerably, what is wanted to-day in industry more than ever before are young men. Men who were fifty-five or fifty years of age when the depression began and who have not yet reached seventy years of age cannot find employment and must be cared for in some way. It does not help our war effort to have the plight of these old people continually before us as a reminder of the callousness of the government in dealing with poverty and destitution. Some little time ago the Vancouver Sun, a newspaper which supports the Liberal party, had an editorial on old age pensions. It was entitled "Fifth Commandment Betrayed at $20 a Month." It said in part:
For the thousands of years since God spoke to Moses that fifth commandment of the mighty decalogue has shone unchallenged. It has been an integral teaching of Christianity.
It then went on to show the amount that an ordinary man and woman adds to the wealth of the country during his or her forty years or so of productive life, and it continued:
And for this service to their country and their fellow men, this man and woman will, if

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
in need near the journey's end, receive $20 a month-sixty-six cents a day. They are to live on that. They are to maintain their little home-and thus spend their last years in peace.
That is really not good enough. Although we are at war and although the war makes tremendous demands upon our productive effort, still the resources of this country are sufficient, if properly organized, to enable us not only to carry on and double our war effort, but to ensure a decent standard of living to every man, woman and child in the dominion. Therefore there is no reason in the world why our old people should have to continue to live in the destitution that many of them are living in now.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a war budget, and before I sit down I wish to say something about the war. I am not going to criticize what we have done or failed to do. The times are too critical for anything of that kind. Indeed, I am too anxious to win this war for me to engage in futile criticism. I am interested in defeating Hitlerism and in maintaining for ourselves and the world those principles for which we are fighting in this war. How best we can do that is a problem which I think occupies every waking hour of every serious man and woman in the Dominion of Canada to-day.
There are so many things to be done besides the drilling of men and the production of munitions. These, of course, are of great importance. But Hitler does not win his victories by these means alone, and it would be well if we, too, gave some thought to other phases of modern warfare.
The German nazis have two things which we must acquire for ourselves if we are going to defeat them. These two things are: first, unification of purpose, and second, the tools and equipment which we are to use in the war. We are doing a great deal in the latter direction, but I think a great deal of our difficulty, and a great deal of the difficulty of nil the democracies, both before and since the war started, was that there was no unification of purpose within their countries.
Hitler knows what he wants. He has had a clear picture of it in his mind for the past twenty years. What does he want? He wants power and he wants conquest. What he will do with that power and with that conquest when he gets it, he has not yet -stopped to think. Indeed he cannot stop to think what he is ultimately going to do, because he has as yet set no limits to the power and territory which he aims to acquire. Even a superficial examination of Hitler's record since he came into power will convince Anyone who takes the trouble to look into it
that what I have said is right, that Hitler has one purpose-power for himself and for the German nation.
From the very beginning he organized his campaign with masterly, if diabolical, ingenuity. He used every passion and emotion, the worthy as well as the unworthy, among his friends and among his enemies for his foul purpose. In Germany itself, and outside Germany as well, he said to the rich: "I will save you from the trade unions, from the socialists and the communists". They believed him, and they financed him.
To the middle class and the professional classes, he said: "I will save you from the trusts, the chain stores, the monopolies, and above all from the Jews who are taking far too large a share of the positions and the wealth which are rightly yours". And they believed him.
To the farmers and small business men, he said: "Your enemy is international finance; I will put them in their places and make you the masters". And they believed him.
To the youth and unorganized workers and the unemployed of Germany, he said: "You have been betrayed by the social democrats who are working in league with the capitalist class; I will give you work; I will give you a share in the government of the country; I will give you outlets for your energy and for your creative skills." And they believed him. To some extent he has kept this promise; so much has he kept it that to-day the youth of Germany are a menace to the world.
To the returned soldiers and to the military caste he said: "You were not defeated in the field; you were betrayed by an incompetent and corrupt government; I will give you an opportunity to show the world that the German soldier is unbeatable." And they believed him. His technique was the essence of simplicity. He made promises to everybody and he broke every one of them.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that what you want us to do?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I want you to keep your promises but you have not done so.
Everyone has some grievance, and the nazis always have a sovereign remedy. Each of the classes or groups that I have mentioned believed that the nazis were working for the interests of his particular class or group.
Hitler is now doing with nations what he formerly did with groups and individuals within Germany. He will get what he wants by cajolery. If not, will get it by threats, and if that is not enough, he will take it with tanks and dive bombers.
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

He never moves until he is ready, and when he does move, he has overwhelming force at his command. It seems to me then that if we are going to defeat Hitler, the first thing to be done is to put before the people a picture of the world for which we are planning after Hitler is defeated. We must have before us a picture of the new world for which we are fighting, because we cannot struggle and sacrifice enthusiastically and determinedly for something that we are not clear about; for things about which there is a conflict of opinion even among our leaders. To say that we are fighting for the destruction of nazism and fascism is not enough.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was trying to put in words what I thought we had to do if we were to win the war. I mentioned a number of things, and I was just saying that it was not enough to say that we are fighting for the destruction of nazism or fascism; neither is it enough to say that this is a struggle for the preservation of freedom, liberty, democracy and other such desirable things. We must make these words real facts in our every day lives, not for some but for all. They must stand out, bold and clear, as so many of the good things of life now. In my opinion, it is sheer impertinence to tell a man who is trying to maintain a home and family on an impossible wage and who, if caught trying to organize with his fellows to better his condition, may be instantly dismissed from his employment, that he has great stakes in the fight to destroy Hitlerism. As a matter of fact, such a man is too close to the essence of Hitlerism to believe you.
There is, indeed, much that is good in democratic society, much that is worth while saving even for the lowliest; but it is no wonder it is hard to convince many of the hundreds of thousands who for the past ten years have suffered the miseries of the damned that these benefits have reached down to them. I have already pointed out how Hitler won the confidence of the German people. The promises he made could not, of course, be kept because they contradicted one another. Consequently, in order to keep his dupes quiet he has had to continue to make more promises. The last he has made to the German people is that when they have conquered the world they will have the world's peoples for their slaves. That is the picture they have before them to-day.
[Me. Maclnnis.]
The democracies, however, in my opinion can still defeat the nazi hordes if they are willing to pay the price. The price is more democracy. We must extend freedom. We must make the common, ordinary working man feel that he is not a mere worker, a mere hand in a mill or a factory, but that he is an important person in the community and that the country is interested in his welfare. To acquire the force and unity of purpose to win this war, we shall have to do certain things. We must get clear in our minds that the present struggle is not only a war; it is a world revolution. Hitler never ceases to tell his people that. We must realize that we can never go back to conditions as they were before the war began. We either go forward to a more perfect democracy than we ever had before or go backward to fascism. We must remember that democracy can live only by growing; that if we at any time try to set a period to it, to say, "Thus far you shall go and no farther", then we have taken the first step on the road to fascism.
The second thing that must be done is to put forward a positive programme of what we are fighting for. This programme obviously cannot be a blueprint of a new social order. It must, however, provide measures of social betterment, and, above all, it must adopt humane social attitudes toward economic problems. It must state in clear terms what will be done as soon as normal conditions are restored. It should and it must, if we are to succeed, be able to tell the young men who are to-day fighting the battle in the field, in the air, on the sea, the men and the women who are fighting in the mines, on the farms, in the mills and factories behind the lines, that they and their brothers and sisters will not have to go back to the life that was theirs between 1930 and 1940. In fact, such a programme must bring the benefits of democracy so close to the poorest of our people that they will be so obvious that the people will be prepared to fight for them and, if necessary die for them.
We must drastically cut the spread in income and opportunity which now exists among our .people. The adoption of this programme by our government would give the principles for which we are fighting, or for which we say we are fighting, more meaning in the eyes of the people than they now have. Let us not forget that we are in this war because the ruling classes and the wealthy classes of the countries of Europe preferred their class privileges to democracy. They were prepared to build up Hitler. They did build up Hitler on his promise to destroy the trade unions and the socialist movement.

The Budget-Mr. Jackman
We shall have to get it into our heads, therefore, -that we cannot organize effectively to win this war while our energies and efforts are hampered by sectional interest and -class strife. We must find ways of resolving our differences in the face of a common and ruthless foe. If we are to win the war and the peace that will follow, and gain for the world an opportunity to build a better -and more glorious future than man has ever before known, we -must begin now and realize before it is too late that we must have the minds and the souls as well as the bodies of men.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would perhaps be surprising to -members of this house, and to many people in Canada, if they were told that financial policies might cause the winning or the loss of a war depending upon whether or not the right or the wrong policies were adopted. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) so ably stated in his budget address on April 29, the financial policy of the government must be directed toward mobilizing the maximum war strength of Canada. The first objective in doing this is to give sufficient financial aid to bring about the full use of our resources and man-power. The second objective is to follow a pay-as-you-go policy as much as possible. This government has followed that policy as far as is practicable. Civilian demands for goods must not be allowed to conflict with war demands. So long as there were unemployed workers it was not likely that the government would have to do very much to restrict the civilian demand, because enough goods could be produced to supply -both civilian needs and the demands of war. Inflation was to be avoided at all costs.
On the assumption that these objectives were the proper ones to be adopted in the management of a country at war, a brief consideration of what has happened and what the financial alternatives were may not be out of place. As is well known, under a profit or enterprise economy, goods or services are brought to the market because there is offered for them a price sufficient to repay the cost of production and to yield some return on the capital employed. The higher the price, the greater the amount brought to market. No one questions the effectiveness of the price mechanism in getting a job done. With the ceaseless hunger of war to be fed, however, there would be a never-ending demand for munitions, and the price would be expected to rise until such time as every factory in the country would be engaged at a good profit on the production of some form of war material.
But the use of such price mechanism is costly and results in mounting costs to the government as well as increasing the general price level and setting in motion the vicious spiral of inflation, with consequent difficulties for all, although to the profit of a favoured few. Particularly was this method hard on those with bonds, savings accounts, insurance policies, annuities and the like, for, with the rising cost of living, fixed dollar incomes did not go so far. Nevertheless the financial hardships and volume of debt created during the last war did not seem to be overwhelming.
This war, being a mechanized one, is a much more costly war. The alternative method of financing the war, namely, through a controlled economy-and not only of financing the war but of producing war goods-was adopted. That is undoubtedly an experimental method with regard to both doing a production job and maintaining financial integrity. If sufficient of our national income cannot be diverted through taxation and loans to pay for the war, then it is possible that the cure may be worse than the disease. In a long war I can only hope that the hardships will not be greater than those which would have been produced under a free economy.
On more than one occasion we have heard in this house the eminent British economist, John Maynard Keynes, cited as an expert in monetary matters. In the last budget recently brought down in the United Kingdom, a policy which he has been advocating for some time, namely, that of compulsory savings-although I believe another name is given to itr-was adopted. I should like to quote from a book he wrote some years ago called "Treatise on Money." He has this to say about war finance:
At such a time-
That is, a time of war.
-it is necessary to direct productive resources of all kinds from one employment to another on a large scale and as rapidly as possible.
That is to say, we must change over from a peace-time economy to a war-time economy and change our factories from making peace goods to making war goods, and he says that must be done on a large scale and as rapidly as possible. He continues:
It would be next door to impossible to achieve this except by invoking the assistance of the price mechanism, namely, by placing credit facilities at the disposal of the new employments and allowing them to bid for productive resources against the old employments-
In other words the new war industries must be allowed to outbid the old peace-time industries for the services of labour and material.
-thus allowing some measure of income inflation. Any government which, in the
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

The Budget-Mr. Raymond

called experts, final determination must be made by those responsible to the people. That obligation can be discharged only through consideration of fiscal policies in a committee empowered to call witnesses, and thus to know, first, something of the possible ways and means of raising the revenue and, then, to recommend to this house those proposals which are considered to be in the best interests of Canada.
In the resolution stage I hope to set forth the injustice of the administration in not allowing the $400 exemption to foster-parents of British children, also in imposing the ten per cent passenger transportation tax on soldiers' railway fares. I consider the first to be unpatriotic and the second to be unjust, if not subversive. I protest also against the tax on sugar as being contrary to the welfare of the people. May I here remind the minister that there are other ways and means of raising the revenue without committing gross injustice upon certain of our people whose incomes, notwithstanding the increases of which we have heard in the total national income, are still so low that they find it difficult to get three square meals a day.
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauharnois-Laprairie). Mr. Speaker, in view of some observations made this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), I wish to make a short statement. In September, 1939, the question of the participation of Canada in the present war was submitted to parliament to decide. I then advocated a benevolent neutrality and suggested that a plebiscite should be taken. My views were not accepted and parliament decided in favour of participation. Since then, a majority of the Canadian people have ratified the decision of parliament in the last general election held in March, 1940.
The question now is not one of neutrality but of the degree of participation, and that is what I discussed yesterday. Some have opposite views. Some advocate conscription, to which, I repeat, I am opposed. As I said yesterday, the whole of Canada has, at the polls, unequivocally condemned conscription. I added also: We have no right in a democracy to ignore the sentiment of the people so clearly expressed. To do so would be to expose ourselves to a calamity worse than war. This afternoon, the Minister of Justice said that in my speech yesterday I still advocated a policy of neutrality. He certainly misinterpreted my remarks. I consider that this matter has been decided already by the people of Canada. Inasmuch as I expect others to respect the expression of sentiment of the Canadian people, I do respect it myself.

May I conclude by asking those wffio, like the Gazette of Montreal, persist in asking for conscription, to respect the sentiment of the Canadian people so unequivocally expressed in voting against conscription at the general election of 1940?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not disposed to take up very much of the time of the house, or to delay proceedings in order to make what might appear to be a needless speech, but there are one or two matters to which I wish to refer and which I trust, Mr. Speaker, you will regard as relevant to this debate.
I shall not at the outset attempt to follow the long, winding and rather narrow financial trail traversed by the hon. member for Rose-dale (Mr. Jackman) who preceded me, because I feel that, like himself, I might become bewildered and return from the hunt with nothing to offer.
The discussions throughout the sessions of this parliament have borne a close relationship to our war effort, and that is only natural when we are facing in Canada at the present time an all-time crisis. The emergency makes our war effort our paramount concern, because we see in Europe to-day the greatest tragedy of carnage the world has ever seen, and the ghosts of that tragedy hover over our very doors.
From time to time the ministers upon whom the responsibility rests of organizing and implementing ways and means to provide the men, money, munitions and equipment required for our war effort, have read factual statements to the house showing what has been accomplished to date, and they have offered forecasts of the military prospects. These statements of achievements and the forecasts which the ministers have made have been criticized by some hon. members, particularly those sitting at your honour's remote left. The aggregate of their criticisms has been voluminous and their character varied; but when we consider what a small proportion of their criticisms was constructive, we are forced to the conclusion that they have contributed very little either to expediting or enlarging our war effort. No reasonable man in this house or outside could expect that a project of the magnitude that has been undertaken by this government could be carried through to the end without some venial errors of omission and commission. Canada is not a warlike country, and the twenty-five years which intervened between the termination of the last war and the beginning of this one were not spent by our statesmen and economists in trying to mobilize and prepare for a future war, particularly a war of aggression. Rather they were spending

The Budget-Mr. McGarry
their time in trying to work out the problem of redeeming Canada from its economic ugliness as a result of the last war. In spite, however, of their peaceful temperament, war came and there was nothing for Canada to do but to go to the assistance of Great Britain, that fortress which to-day stands unconquered and undaunted between tyranny and democracy.
I do not intend to pose as a judge and to say definitely what the aggregate of our war effort should be; but when I recollect that only nineteen months ago Canada's military position was one of almost total unpreparedness, and when I consider its military prowess to-day, I am not surprised when I hear or read expressions of admiration and the complimentary plaudits given to this government for its great achievements in mobilizing our resources in men and material for Canada's great war effort.
In this all-out effort it is necessary that every element of our citizenship should sacrifice to the limit. The wage-earner, the salaried man, the business man, must give their earnings and their profits to the point of suffering. The producer must produce more and more. Just at this point let me give this warning to the government. When we ask the producer to produce more, we should take care that we do not take away from him the very facilities he requires to enable him to effect that purpose.
The centralization of war projects unfortunately has left some sections of this country in a position where their earnings or incomes have not increased since the war began. Strategical considerations no doubt govern the location of these war projects. That may be all right, and certain sections of the country may not be penalized thereby; but in sections such as my own constituency, not only are no war projects being carried on, but expenditures for ordinary public works have been withheld necessarily, on the ground of war economy, and that has left us dependent almost entirely upon emergency public works. This condition reduces the people in those sections of the country almost to the standard of a relief unit. This is a matter which the government should consider, because these conditions, if they are allowed to persist, will lead to a discontented and discouraged people who, if the war lasts too long, will lose their ardency in the cause. After all, we can scarcely call that a true democracy which does not accord to every citizen in every stratum of life at least a decent living.
I have particularly in mind one section of producers, the fishermen, who comprise about one-fifth of the .population of my constituency. It is essential that they should produce,
and the fishermen in my constituency, in industry, honesty and hardihood will take second place to no other element in the community. I hope I shall not be charged with being too regional, but this is really a matter of importance. In this regard I am speaking for one-fifth of the population of my constituency. In the district of Cheticamp we had a gypsum mine in operation. It absorbed about 100 of our fishermen, but it has been closed down owing to the war, because bottoms could not be obtained for shipping out the product. The result is that 100 men have gone back to fishing. These fishermen pursue their industry in small boats. Two. years ago we had a life-boat at Cheticamp-for the protection of these fishermen in going to and from their fishing grounds. This gave them security so that they would venture out on days that were not altogether propitious, because they had an assurance of protection. Since that boat has been taken away, the productivity of these fishermen declined last year almost fifty per cent, for the simple reason that these men, who had only small craft, refused to go to the fishing grounds except on extremely fine days. If anything happened on their way to or from their fishing grounds they knew they had nothing to rely on for protection.
This is a small matter. These boats could be maintained at a cost of a very few hundred dollars, and it would render a wonderful service to these men. The fishermen feel that they are in a paradoxical position. They are asked to produce, and at the same time they are deprived of the means of facilitating production. I am not criticizing the government in this connection, but I know whereof I speak. I know the feeling that prevails in that section. If we are to have that unity which is so desirable in this great struggle, we must remove any element of discontent that may exist among the people. No section should feel that there is any reason for them to be dissatisfied.
There is another matter to which this government should pay particular attention. I know that they do, and I mention the matter merely to emphasize its importance. I refer to the health of our people. The health of a people is the wealth of that people. That is an old adage; this is a truism. Certainly it is as true to-day as it ever was, because the lives of the people, whether in peace or in war, are of the greatest concern to the individual as well as to the state. A man-and the same is true of a woman or a child-is in good health if his organs function properly, and no man can satisfactorily fill any position he holds unless that condition is satisfied.
The Budget-Mr. McGarry

Therefore this is one point which this or any other government should bear in mind.
The profession of which I happen to be a humble member has long since given up the erroneous idea that it exists merely for the purpose of treating the sick. Fortunately for ourselves and the public, we have realized that there is another phase of medicine which is far more important than the curative, and that is public health for the general good of the community. Nothing designed for this purpose can function satisfactorily unless we have, first, the cooperation of the public and, second, a government that will furnish adequate means to carry out a programme- not only to maintain it but to enhance it, if possible.
I wish to congratulate the government upon the efforts they so promptly put forth at the very outset of the war. I refer particularly to the war-time prices and trade board. As a result of that and of the persistence *with which its objects have been put into practice, we have not that hoarding and [DOT]consequent profiteering which obtained in the last war. We all remember the orgy of profiteering that went on in the war of 1914-18. The efforts of the war-time prices and trade *board not only have been beneficial so far as the prosecution of the war is concerned, but will prove an important factor in the time of reconstruction at the close of the war. Some people will argue that we should not consider the aftermath of the war, and I admit that while our principal thought and purpose in Canada to-day should be the successful prosecution of the war, at the same time I suggest that, without detracting one iota from this high purpose, we must keep in mind the time when our men who are now engaged in making implements of destruction and of death, will revert to the positions they held in private life.
There should be some reorganization during the process of organizing for the war. We should look to the time when price levels will fall from the altitudes of war time to the more stable basis of peace. There is a trend of continuity going through the process of war and peace, and personally I believe that the foundation of a proper reorganization after the war is an intelligent organization of the war process itself.
At the present time matters are looking dark in the east, but we are not discouraged. We feel that England's military record will be unbroken, and we know that she always wins the last battle. The ultimate battle will be on the Atlantic, and I do not think anyone doubts what the outcome of that deciding struggle will be.
I have the honour to represent a constituency in Nova Scotia. In that province

the truest and fullest expression of national spirit exists, and the fulfilment of that spirit will not be something brought about by might or power. That national spirit is the will to act and to do things. This is the third budget of this war. While we realize that the manufacture of material weapons of war is important, we must also remember that it is just as important to have a people so imbued with the determination to succeed that they will follow that trumpet which to date has never sounded a retreat.
My purpose in mentioning some of these local matters was not one of criticism but merely to emphasize a few matters to which I think it would be well for the government or some department of the government to give a little attention. We in Nova Scotia are not blessed with as many war projects as other sections of the dominion. Having such an abundance of coal and steel, we sometimes wonder, when we see projects in other sections where the cost of freight is very high and, therefore, to my mind manufacturing costs would be higher than in the maritime provinces, why we have not more of such projects. It is possible that the vulnerability of our position causes it to be regarded as unsafe for military plants; but I notice that in England almost all the war plants are at vulnerable points, and in the United States I believe eighty-five per cent of their war plants are at vulnerable points. Any part of Canada will be vulnerable if the British fleet is driven from the seas. When that happens, the relative location of war plants will not make much difference. We feel, however, that the ministers who have to deal with this matter are possibly taking wise precautions, but I suggest that we watch very carefully that in this distribution of favours there are no step-children in this national family. It seems that only in war and in national calamities the worth of the little province of Nova Scotia economically and strategically is recognized. On account of the fact that we are not getting as large a proportion of military projects as we think we should, the government should keep in mind matters such as those of which I have spoken, where certain sections of the country are being penalized, and see to it that some compensation is made in order to bring our wage-earners and others up to a standard of living similar to that of those whose fortune it is to live in busier sections.
The most important factor in this whole war effort is unity, and unless we have a contented people we cannot have absolute unity. In other words, we should see to it that that life-line which goes to the British

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
fortress which to-day is the last bastion of liberty in Europe, that life-line which extends to Nova Scotia, that long wharf of north America, that spearhead of attack against the Berlin beast and the jackal of Italy, shall remain unbroken until the end of this conflict, so that the powers of democracy, liberty and freedom shall prevail over the powers of darkness whose designs are nothing less than to destroy everything that is worth while and spiritual in man.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Representing the men of the soil, men who built the great Canadian west, men who form the very foundation of our national economy, men who are shouldering a great portion of our national tax burden-the men who are commonly known by that unromantic name "farmers", I am privileged, indeed, in this debate, to add my word on their behalf.
Last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) brought down another orthodox budget. In it he did not forget to impose a new levy of additional taxation upon our farmers, who are least able to pay. Notwithstanding the unhappy financial position of our farmers, the minister still seems to think that a heavier burden should be placed upon them.
To make my stand clear, I wish to say that we all realize that in time of war our taxes must of necessity be higher than in time of peace, and that all our people should gladly share in the burden. Nevertheless we have heard so much from this government about its endeavours to distribute additional taxation evenly, and upon those who can best bear it. The additional tax on gasoline purchased by our farmers fails to convince me that it could possibly be helpful to our farmers, without mentioning other new indirect taxes which will further reduce the purchasing power of our farming population.
The farmer does not expect to make a profit out of this war, but he does expect this government to help him to carry on without getting further into debt. He also expects this government to place him in a position to be able to contribute his maximum to the winning of the war. I therefore propose, and feel it my duty, to give this house a more or less complete resume of the economic position of our farmers, and to point out their problems and the method by which at least some of them could be remedied; that is, if we expect our farmers to contribute their maximum to the winning of the war.
In addition to what was said on the subject of agriculture, last week, on the motion of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and which was directed mostly to the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce, I wish
to deal with matters pertaining to the economic position of agriculture which concern other departments, including the Department of Finance. I should like again to remind this house that approximately one-third of our total Canadian population depend upon agriculture for their living. I believe, therefore, that we should all agree that the agricultural problem in Canada is one of prime importance, second only to our war effort, for Canada is primarily and fundamentally an agricultural country.
Among the many problems facing the Canadian farmer to-day, and more particularly the western Canadian farmer, I wish to deal briefly with the following:
1.	Adaptation to fast-changing conditions.
2.	The debt problem.
3.	High interest rates on private debts.
4.	Inadequate freight rate structure.
5.	Low prices on farm produce.
6.	Marketing possibilities.
7.	Price of manufactured goods to the farmer.
8.	Increased and heavy tax burden.
9.	Lack of purchasing power in the hands of the people.
10.	Low standard of living.
11.	Constant rise in the cost of living in relation to income.
12.	Inadequacy of the present debt-creating system.
13.	Lack of a positive and aggressive national agricultural policy.
14.	The post-war period.
First let me deal with the ever-changing conditions to which the farmer must be continually adapting himself in order to survive. During the last several decades the position of the farmer has been gradually changing from one of economic independence to one of economic dependence and centralization, making it possible for the money barons to get a firm strangle-hold on his security. On the one hand, technological development ha* been a blessing to the farmer, inasmuch as it. has lightened the burden of his physical labours and added to the speed and efficiency of production; but on the other hand, labouring under the disadvantages of the orthodox financial system, the farmer has become the unfortunate prey of financial institutions.
Besides the swift technological changes, the contemporary farmer is surviving two of the greatest wars the world has ever known, and, in addition, he is still struggling with the effects of twelve years of the worst economic dislocation in our history. As a consequence of this economic dilemma, the farmer has been forced to accumulate huge debts at high rates of interest, which has placed him in an
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

even less enviable position. It went something like this. The farmer had to mortgage his farm in order to buy a tractor. He then had to mortgage the tractor in order to build a garage. Finally he had to mortgage the garage in order to buy gasoline. So went the merry-go-round.
Perhaps it might be of interest to hon. members to learn the amount of the average private indebtedness of an individual farmholding in western Canada. In stable settlements an individual farmer is, on the average, carrying a private debt load of $5,000. A further analysis of the debt situation shows that even in pioneering and quite recent settlements, such as the Peace river district in Alberta, the total private indebtedness of an individual farmer has, on the average, reached the $2,000 mark. If time permitted, I could produce figures showing how many farm-holders in these same areas are valued at less than $5,000 and $2,000 respectively.
I wonder how many of us have yet realized that a great part of our accumulated debt is not made up of original loans. In many instances, those have been repaid over and over again. It is the accumulation of interest that keeps our people in debt and has been responsible for many foreclosures in western Canada. Let me stress this point. In many instances the original debts have been repaid several times in our generation; that statement may be verified by examining almost any mortgage-debt. In reality, this situation has virtually reduced the farmer's status to that of a tenant of the vested interests. It has further resulted in a lack of economic security. This, in my opinion, constitutes a real threat to our agricultural industry, which forms the very basis of our national economy. The greatest danger of all, however, lies in the fact that land ownership is gradually passing from the hands of the farmers to those of financial institutions and centralized control. This condition is one of the greatest threats to practical economic democracy, for that tendency is on the up-grade each year.
No one can deny that our federal governments of the last twelve years, in the main, should be held responsible for permitting this condition to become so aggravated. Because of their hopeless failure to handle the debt problem satisfactorily, our people have, for many years, been subjected to exploitation and abuse by the moneyed interests. The so-called debt adjustments proved, in most instances, to be debt maladjustments; yet, in the face of all this, the federal government and the courts have disallowed or held ultra vires six of the Alberta debt acts which were passed for the

sole purpose of giving the people of that province the protection they should have been given by the federal government. The most consistent excuse given by this government for disallowing those acts was to the effect that the government of Alberta was invading the field of federal jurisdiction. If that be so, Mr. Speaker, the federal government itself should have passed the necessary and adequate debt legislation so that our people could have had the protection they required, for, as we know, financial institutions have had no heart in dealing with their debtors. The governments to which I have already referred stood by and watched as financial institutions squeezed the very economic lifeblood out of our defenceless farmers of western Canada; and as a reward for their long years of toil, many farmers were turned out on the road. Fortunately, the people of Alberta have fared better during the last few years under the Social Credit government. Premier William Aberhart and his cabinet may well be proud of their record in this respect. As I have already indicated, they have done their level best in trying to save thousands of families from destitution.
This government will say, of course, that it has taken care of the debt situation by using the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Let me say at once that I have yet to find a settlement made under this act which turned out satisfactorily to the farmer. Those hon. members who have been asked, at one time or another, to assist farmers in their own constituencies, to save them from foreclosure, know very well how hard it is to persuade the creditor to be human. If the farmer fails to meet his payment on time, even for reasons beyond his control, he is immediately branded as dishonest, as not keeping his word; he is told he should be ashamed of himself, that he is not fit to be farming, and the like. This gives the company a distinct advantage in its attempt to throw the farmer off his land. Let us then ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, why should a farmer shiver at the very sound of the name of a trust or a security company? Where does the trust or security come in? The fact of the matter is, that the farmer is always offered an umbrella when the sun shines, but when it begins to rain, the money-man asks the farmer to give back the umbrella. That is what is called a sound financial set-up. Yes, it is sound, and nothing but sound, and it is designed to serve the few, not the many.
Let me tell this government that it could help our farmers in more ways than one, and especially at the present time when foreign markets for our wheat are partly closed.

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
Adjust and readjust the farmers' debts and you will have solved half their problems. Then the farmer will be in a better position to stand additional taxation.
Let us now examine the chances that a farmer has to extricate himself from this complex situation. His only source of revenue comes from the sale of his produce; he receives no income from bonds or other investments. In time of war, the farmer is faced with the problem of partly closed markets, and he therefore cannot make a sale of his principal product. In time of peace, the affairs of the country are so managed that unemployment is rampant, the purchasing power of the people is reduced, and underconsumption follows. This underconsumption is usually termed by politicians and other financial sycophants as "overproduction" or "surpluses." Finally, when the farmer does manage to sell some of his produce, he is forced to sell it at a price which is usually below the cost of production. Therefore, what incentive has the farmer to produce?
I wish to emphasize this point, that our farmers have been placed in the most impossible situation. If they do not produce they cannot exist, let alone live; but the more they produce, the poorer they become. In other words, the fruits of their own labours make them poor and miserable.
With respect to this "overproduction" or "surplus" idea, about which we hear so much from orthodox thinkers, I will say that that condition hardly ever exists. Let me illustrate the point. Less than a year ago this government told us that we had a "surplus" or an "overproduction" of butter in Canada. An interesting article appeared in the November issue of the Canadian Dairy and Ice Cream Journal. This article was written by Charlotte I. Johnson, who is employed by the federal Department of Agriculture, economics branch, and she fold us how the government had distributed all the surplus Canadian . butter. Hon. members will recall that the government issued to relief recipients and low-income families blue vouchers with which they could purchase additional amounts of butter. We were told that 3.081.697 pounds of butter were distributed in this wray. After that butler was distributed, there were still thousands of low-income families in Canada who did not have enough.
The point is that there never was a surplus or an overproduction of butter in Canada. But the fact of the matter is that our people did not have enough purchasing pow'er with which to buy. This year the same government tells us to go easy on butter because we have not enough of it. But the truth of
the matter is that the government showed a lack of foresight or vision for even a few months ahead. I must be frank and say that that type of policy is not good enough to suit either the consumer or the producer. I might say also that if the government took the trouble and saw to it that the farmer received a fair price for his butter, our farmers could produce more butter than we need. The same principle applies to other commodities of which it is said that we have either a shortage or a surplus.
Let me now deal with our markets. We are usually led to believe that our economy wholly depends upon our export trade. That has been the most consistent argument this government has advanced in shielding its ineffective marketing policy. We are told over and over again that a farmer could not get a reasonable price for his produce because we depend upon foreign markets, and that since those markets are partly closed for our major commodity, namely, wheat, the Canadian people cannot expect to have enough of the things of which we have an abundance. This type of reasoning is simply below anyone's dignity to advance; and yet our people have been fed with that kind of concentrated nonsense right along.
Let us now examine the true state of the situation. Let me point out that our farmers' markets are not wholly dependent upon our foreign trade. As a matter of fact, our farmers could be making a comfortable living and could contribute much more to our war effort if the government took the trouble to help them get a fair return for their produce-produce which is sold on our home markets, right here in Canada. At page 126 of a booklet entitled "The Case for Organized Empire Migration", written by Brigadier-General Hornby in May, 1937, we find the following:
Speaking generally there is a good market in Canada for all farm produce. The question of market facilities must not be confused with the question of price. It is the price on farm produce which has hit the farmer so hard. Our local markets may be expected to improve when and as employment improves, the price on agricultural products being dependent on the purchasing power of the masses, who are the largest consumers of farm products.
In my opinion, this government publication has placed before us the true state of affairs embodied in the above quotation. That is exactly what Social Crediters have been telling this house and the people of Canada for the past six years. Let me give hon. members a table taken from the 1935 "Canada Year Book," which substantiates my argument. The following is the proportion of certain Canadian
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

farm products consumed in Canada, and the greatly smaller percentages exported:

This table shows that our markets are not dependent upon our external trade to as large a degree as we are led to believe. As a matter of fact, the figures almost surprise me. These farm products are almost entirely consumed in Canada. Then, why not give the farmer a fair price in return for these commodities? If he were given fair prices, his trouble would be considerably alleviated. But the farmer is always given the old excuse, and he accepts it in good faith. Social Crediters have been consistently stressing the idea that additional purchasing power must be placed in the hands of our people before a solution to our problems can be found, and, what is more, the Social Crediters have proposed a plan by which that may be done.
The table I have placed on record shows that our domestic market for many of our products is a remarkably good one. Let us then set a fair minimum price on those commodities, and let us do business. In view of the present unsatisfactory economic situation of our farmers, let us give them their long-overdue break. Let us tell them that they have been let down, that they have not been protected as they should have been. Let us tell our farmers that there is no reason in the world why they should not be enjoying a higher standard of living. Let us tell our farmers that they should not be denied, at least, the basic necessities of life, namely, food, clothing and shelter. Why not tell our farmer that he has been the scapegoat right along, and then he will know the truth. This mess may well exist for a time, but there must be an end to it some time.
Let that situation be remedied now, when our farmers are asked to shoulder the heaviest tax burden in Canada's history. Everyone seems to report profits as a result of war activities, but our farmer seems to be singled out as if he were not a part of our national life. Everyone reports profits, and that is what all hon. members in the house should consider. It is the duty of each of us to press the government for results, for, after all. it is only results that count.
Let us now consider another important phase of the same situation. When a farmer buys an

article, he must pay an exorbitant price for it. There is no mention of overproduction or surplus where the manufacturer is concerned. On the other hand, when the farmer sells his produce, he is forced to accept what he is offered. Surely, this state of affairs has not come about as a result of some accident or something of that sort. I should like to read from a letter which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 22, 1941, and which gives a good example of what I am trying to point out. I quote:
Why are apples so expensive now when there is known to be no scarcity? In November, 1939, I paid 99 cents for a bushel of Ontario apples. In January, 1941, I paid $2.25 for a bushel of the same kind and grade.
Since then I have been told that Nova Scotia apples cannot be sent into Ontario, even as gifts, except in small quantities, and that growers in that province are forced to accept ten cents a barrel at the canneries for the best apples. Surely this is an injustice both to the producer and the consumer.
That is just how the injustice comes in. The producer is always told how much he is going to get for his produce, and he is also told how much he will have to pay for the articles sold to him. Invariably there is no relationship between the prices set on the commodities which the farmer has to sell and those which he must buy.
I should like to give an example of the income upon which the farmer must depend. In the annual report of the Department of Agriculture for the year ended March 31, 1939, a table will be found at page 43 showing average farm prices, as follows:

Let me turn now to a comparison of the prices of commodities which the farmer must buy. One glaring example of the lack of

This is where he gets into debt, and few of them ever get out of it. There is the obvious reason why the farmer cannot get out of debt.' It should also be obvious that something must be done to bring about a closer relationship between the prices the farmer gets for his produce and the prices he has to pay to the manufacturer. Farm machinery is one item on the list of instruments of production. Therefore the price of machinery should be cut and controlled. At the present time the farmer is paying an extra ten per cent duty on parts and machinery imported from across the line, and then, in addition, he must pay the exchange on Canadian money. How can the farmer exist under such adverse conditions when all the cards seem to be stacked against him from whatever angle one views the situation?
Incidentally, I might point out that the provincial Social Credit government has been instrumental in reducing the price on parts of farm machinery by fifteen to thirty-five per cent. The provincial government is handling this mass purchasing through the Provincial Marketing Board. In this way the Social Credit government has forced the machine companies to reduce their prices on machine parts. We should like to know now what the federal government has been doing in this respect in the last few years.
We have heard a lot in this house, and we read so much about this inflation bogy. If there is any group in this house which is against inflation or deflation, it certainly is the Social Credit group. Let me point out to hon. members who so often try to ridicule our financial proposals, and who have hopelessly failed to cope with the situation under their own system, how the farmer looks at this idea of inflation. Let us remember that it was the farmer who was inflated by election promises for the past several decades.
From the farrtier's point of view, he is at present experiencing the greatest inflation in Canada's history. To-day he must pay four 14873-170
bushels of wheat for an article which he obtained for one bushel of wheat in 1914. From the financier's point of view, it is the price of wheat that went down, while his dollar remained sound, but from the farmer's point of view, his wheat is as sound as ever. Since his wheat is sold at one-quarter of its value as compared with the past, there is an inflation of 400 per cent so far as he is concerned. After all, we must remember that the banker's certificates were never intended to represent intrinsic value. All money was intended for the purpose of transferring and distributing goods and services when and where required.
This brings to mind the game which the first white traders used to play when Canada was young. A trader would give the Indian a gun if in return he agreed to give him a pile of furs as high as the gun. The trader soon inflated the Indian by ordering the same gun from the manufacturer, but with a longer barrel. In this way the Indian had to give a higher pile of furs for the same type of gun simply because the barrel was longer. The same practice is being carried on here at the present time. The trader is the money-man; the gun is the banker's credit; a pile of wheat has taken the place of the pile of furs, and the farmer is forced to play the part of the Indian.
It is gratifying to know, however, that our farmers are beginning to see the light through this maze of complications. Make no mistake about that!
On top of these evils and handicaps, the farmer is forced to put up with a most unjust and inadequate freight rate structure for long distance hauling. As a matter of fact, he pays double freight. He pays freight on things which he buys and on things which he sells. This further reduces the income of the farmer. On top of it all, a heavy tax burden is thrown in for a good measure, which certainly is not equally distributed according to the ability to pay. As I have already pointed out, the uncontrolled pyramiding of debt coupled with the low income of the farmer results in a standard of living far below that which should be enjoyed by our Canadian people. It should also be remembered that the cost of living is rising steadily from day to day.
Of late, we have heard much in this house as well as from high-salaried government and bank officials of the so-called belt-tightening proposal, and further proposals with respect to cutting down on the purchase of luxury goods. These gentlemen may rest assured that their wishes have been complied with by our farmers for a considerable number of years. Of course, judging from the society columns of our daily press, there is no sign

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

of belt-tightening there. These economics are not applicable to the cream of society, to use the agricultural term "cream."
I believe that I have made it sufficiently clear by my remarks up to this point that a deplorable condition exists among the farmers, and particularly so in the prairie provinces. We should, therefore, all be agreed that immediate steps should be taken toward effecting a solution of our farm problems. The stand which I have taken here to-day is supported by farmers in all sections of Canada, as evidenced by numerous resolutions from various farm and other organizations, as well as by the general commotion with which the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has had personal experience on public platforms.
It follows, therefore, that there are only two logical conclusions which one may draw from an analysis of the present farm situation. The first is, that the present agricultural policy is inadequate, and the second, that the government has not had a positive and aggressive agricultural policy during the term it has held office. Further, I do not hesitate to state that the government's financial policy should accept a larger share of the blame for the shortcomings as a result of which our agricultural industry is suffering.
Coming back to the Minister of Agriculture, I must say, with all due respect for his ability, that the farmers of Canada are demanding an aggressive and a positive agricultural policy. They also believe that their industry is sufficiently important, especially at the present time, to have a full-time Minister of Agriculture. As a matter of fact, it is an overtime job at the present time for any man. I might add that the Department of National War Services is also a full-time job, and half the minister for each department is not good enough, as may be judged by the way in which some of our agricultural problems are being handled at present.
Let me stress this fact:	The government
must adopt an agricultural policy which will not only remedy a more immediate aggravating situation, but that it also be far-seeing enough to prepare for the post-war period.
Let me summrize: The government must of necessity assist our farmers in meeting the changing conditions to make it possible for the agricultural industry once more to become a way of making a living and to enable our farmers to contribute their maximum to our war effort. This may be done by:
1.	Amending the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, or passing a new debt act, as well as amending the interest rates act for the purpose of reviewing and equitably adjusting,
TMr. Hlynka.]
in the light of present conditions, all private debts in western Canada. I suggest that all outstanding debts be paid in goods, at standardized price values. That price must be the cost of production, plus at least five per cent. I also suggest that all the interest on all outstanding private debts be suspended and cancelled for the duration of the war; and for at least one year thereafter. It must be remembered that most of these private debts were contracted under highly speculative conditions, and as a result the farmer has become a heavy loser.
2.	I propose that compounding of interest be done away with altogether; for whoever invented the idea of compound interest could not have had the welfare of the people at heart. Compounding of interest is in reality a penalty, a punishment for failing to pay; it is the pound of flesh. Under conditions such as we have to-day, why should the farmer be punished for something which is beyond his control?
3.	This government should immediately pass a home-owners' security act for the purpose of prohibiting the foreclosure or sale of homes in Canada for a debt. This act should be patterned upon the act which the Alberta government had passed in 1938 but which was disallowed by the federal government.
4.	The government should adopt a production tax plan so that our farmers would pay their taxes according to their ability to pay, based upon production.
5.	And lastly, may I urge the government, as others have, to create the necessary amount of credit through the Bank of Canada to buy all the foodstuffs that Britain needs and all that we can spare, and give them to the British people free of charge. This should be kept up for the duration of the war. Of course, the prehistoric orthodox minds will maintain and argue that we have not the money, but that argument will not stand up against logic and common sense in time of war when this nation is fighting for its very existence. The farmer should be paid a fair price for his produce, and the British people should get the necessary aid they need. If this government bluntly refuses to accept this proposal, let it use its own system of doing it, but it must be done. Anything short of this is not good enough.
Such action on our part would have not only material significance but also the greatest moral significance imaginable.
In conclusion, may I just mention that the United States, under the leasfe-Iend bill, have put us to shame in this respect. The United States government will be suppbdng Great

The Budget-Mr. Leclerc
Britain with 81,350,000,000 worth of foodstuffs. The Argentine has donated a considerable amount of beef, and it should be remembered that those two countries do not expect to get paid for these things either. They know there will be a British market after the war. Canada has managed to negotiate trade agreements with Britain at a time when Britain needs all her finances to pay for he freedom, and for ours. What an accomplishment that was in the most critical moment of British history! Let us then do all in our power to save the British commonwealth of nations rather than try to save the orthodox financial system which has failed to serve the needs of the majority of our people. If we do that, we need have no fear of the outcome of the future.
