subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his performance of an extremely difficult job, a job of imposing taxation so heavy that he was appalled by his own words. In the light of recent events, however, we must look at the general position in which we find ourselves to-day. We must look at ourselves in the light of the changed picture. We must look at ourselves since the campaign in Greece,, the battle of Britain, the Hyde Park convention, the lease-lend bill and the battle of the Atlantic. All these have a vital effect on us here in this chamber to-night.
The first thing that we have learned is, I believe, the fallacy of limited man-power. The battle of Greece has shown us that we need all the man-power we can get in Canada. We must now consider, not what our maximum military effort must be, but what our minimum military effort must be immediately. Men and machines, not men or machines; both are needed. It is almost criminal folly to delude ourselves into thinking that we are going to be able to get through this war without large military forces. At the battle of Mount Olympus the gallant Australian troops were outnumbered, in some instances twenty-five to one. Are we going to continue to let these things happen? If we do, the words of warning spoken yesterday by the Prime Minister of Australia have fallen on deaf ears. We must appreciate, we must understand the power of the enemy. It is a first and cardinal rule that we must not underestimate the enemy we are fighting.
We must look first at our minimum military effort, and I have this to suggest in the light of the battle of Greece; that we need four infantry divisions, and with each division at complete armoured brigade and complete artillery units. Besides that, I suggest that we need two complete armoured divisions. We must be able to maintain in Canada in training complete reinforcements for these formations, assuming an annual wastage of one-third. That I submit is, in the light of recent events, the minimum commitment that we can be called upon to complete.
For Canadian coast defence, vulnerable point duty guards, et cetera, should be composed
26SS
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

of B, C, and even D category men; these can largely be recruited from veteran guard companies. Women must be trained and used foi non-combatant work in Canada and possibly abroad. We are going to need every single able-bodied Canadian; let us realize that and realize it now.
Let us see what this would entail. An infantry division is approximately 17,000 men. For safety, let us say 20,000. An armoured brigade is approximately 3,000 men. The auxiliary corps troops are approximately 2,000. Therefore a division such as I have suggested, complete with armoured brigade, would equal about 25,000 men. Four divisions, four armoured brigades, mean about 100,000 men. An armoured division for convenience can be said to be made up of 15,000 men; with specialists and workshops let us increase it to 17,500; two armoured divisions, therefore, amount to about 35,000 men. These formations total, roughly, 135,000 active personnel. 'Let us add, for simplicity, 15,000 artillery; this would mean an active fighting force of 150,000. If we take reinforcements at one-third, we commit ourselves in the coming year to an army of 200.000 men. Add to this an air force of 60,000, of which only a fraction are for overseas, and the naval service at the very maximum-I put this extremely high -of 40,000. From this we have a demand on our man-power of 300,000 men, a number of whom will certainly be remaining in Canada.
It has been asked, why train men until we have casualties? Thank God that we have had no casualties. But we must expect them, and the time to expect them and prepare for them is now. To-day every fighting man is an expert, a specialist, and he takes time to train. If he becomes a casualty, he cannot be replaced by a raw recruit. That recruit must be a trained man, and the time to train the reinforcements is before the original soldier becomes a casualty, not afterwards. That time is now.
There is one other point, and it is an extremely important one, namely, that the surest way to have a long casualty list is to send untrained troops against the enemy. If we compare the effort I have suggested with that of Germany, who is reported1 to have at her disposal 225 divisions, and England with between 80 and 100 divisions of the same size as ours-the German division is somewhat smaller than ours-we shall see that asking Canada for six divisions is indeed a minimum. Compare that with England, with a population of 45 million, raising 80 divisions; Germany, including the people of part of the occupied territory, Czechoslovakia and Austria, with a population of over 100 million with 225 divisions; and

Canada with 11| million population, with six divisions. Surely, if we are going to pretend we are making an all-out war effort, this is not asking too much. I do not need to remind the house that both England and Germany have an air force. And England, thank God, has the Royal Navy.
I come now to the question of munitions, at which I believe we must look in a rather different light since the passage of the lease-lend bill and the Hyde Park conversation. It is, I think, obvious to hon. members that we have been able, in Canada, to do certain things in Canada better than others. Some things we have done well; some things we have not done well. For the sake of brevity I have made three classifications: things we have done well; things we have done moderately well, and things we have done poorly. These are very brief classifications; and some things in one category perhaps should be placed in another. I would suggest to the house that the things in which we have been successful are:	the
manufacture of automatic weapons, anti-aircraft guns, mechanical transport, shells, small arms ammunition, high explosives, steel plate, and the production of raw and refined metal, including aluminium, copper, lead, zinc and gold. We have been moderately successful in the manufacture of training aircraft, ships, mortars, armoured fighting vehicles and antitank guns. We have been poor in the production of fighting and bombing aircraft for actual combat with the enemy, machine tools, field guns, internal combustion engines, and heavy ordnance such as large calibre naval and military artillery.
This is only an extremely limited list; and, as I have said, some of the items in one category perhaps should be placed in others. The general idea is that we are doing some things better than others. The reason for this is our national economy. In the light of our present knowledge, it is obviously fantastic to expect us in Canada to create a large aircraft industry building combat machines. It is also ridiculous to expect us to manufacture naval rifles of 9, 14, 15 or 16-inch calibre. We have not the forges or the personnel, which it takes years to train, and which some authorities consider it requires generations to train. We must approach our munitions problem from the scientific angle of man-hours. The question to be asked is, how many man-hours to produce a certain article in Canada, how many in England and how many in the United States? The question of cost must be given some consideration, but in a desperate

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
struggle such as that in which we are now engaged the time factor far outweighs all other considerations.
There is one further matter which is of interest here with regard to aircraft and any air training scheme. The essential thing about training a man to fly is to put him in a flying machine and to put that flying machine in the air. In any training scheme there are bound to be many crashes. When a machine is crashed, it is useless until it is put back in the air. At present, crashed machines take far too long between the time they are cracked up and the time they fly again. This is a serious bottle-neck. The time a machine is being repaired is wasted time. I suggest to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) that consideration should be given to taking the men now working in the construction of combat and bombing planes and turning them over to the repairing of crashed aircraft. Further, I believe thought should be given to having the repair of training aircraft placed in civilian hands. I feel certain that the air hours per machine per month would be materially increased if this were done. The essential to be remembered is that training aircraft must be kept in the air. Pilots and air crews are not trained on the ground, although they do receive some instruction there. There is a modern adaptation of the old saying about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush. It is that an hour in the air is worth ten on the ground.
I now come a little more specifically to the question of man-power, which must engage the immediate attention of the government. I have already suggested what I believe should be our minimum commitment abroad in connection with the army. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has said that we need 22,000 men immediately, and that a recruiting drive is to be put on in order to get them. I hope that drive will be successful. I cannot go into details concerning this, since it is a matter on which I have official information; however, I can say that my opinion, as a member of this house, is that the method to be employed is most unsatisfactory. Recruiting is a military matter; and to resort to pep talks by prominent citizens in order to induce men to do their duty is a sad reflection on the state of apathy all across Canada, the responsibility for which rests solely on the shoulders of the government. The sober fact, Mr. Speaker, is that we need every able-bodied man, woman and child in Canada and we need them now; not to-morrow, or next week, or in the fall, but now, this very hour. The situation brooks no delay. It must be answered here in this house, and it must be answered now.
The question is: What is the government going to do if it does not get the recruits it needs for the armed forces? We who are in the army do what we are told; we obey orders. We do not do what we would like to do or go where we want to go; the time we do things is the appointed time, and the method is the appointed method. We do these things cheerfully and quickly. This is what is called discipline; the better the discipline, the better the army. So it is with nations. A happy nation is a well disciplined one. A well disciplined nation is a free nation. Where you have gangsters and lawbreakers, you have harsh laws and penalties. Where you have a happy, peaceful, free people, there you have few restrictive laws and light penalties. Any land where "verboten" is always in sight, and where the death penalty is meted out for listening to the wrong radio station, is an undisciplined land. The myth of Germany being a well disciplined country is one of the most damnable fallacies ever invented. The German is like his government and like the brazen nazi horde; he is a gangster at heart. He is ruled by fear; he understands fear, and fear alone.
I mention this subject of discipline because most people have an entirely wrong understanding of the word. The army defines "discipline" as a willing, prompt and implicit obedience to senior authority charged with responsibility. That senior authority in Canada is the federal government. There is one warning that the army issues to those in whom it vests authority. It is that a leader must, above all, have the confidence of his men, who must be resolutely and courageously led. If the government carries on that instruction, we need have no fear for the future of the armed forces.
Having briefly discussed the problem now facing us, we come to the rather uninteresting task of method or, shall we say, the carrying out of our project. The government having said that the situation is serious, in fact very serious, they must have some scheme or plan of operation. I hope they have. They may, however, be unaware of certain conditions common in Canada to-day. This may be a lack of information, or it may be wilful ignorance. The country may be under the impression that we had a registration of manpower during the month of August, 1940. It may believe that this legislation may have had a check on the available and potential reserves of the country. If that is so, let me hasten to disabuse this house of any such idea.
Like many hon. members I used to believe what I was told by ministers of the crown. This was, I found, due to a naive gullibility.
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

I know better now. I believe the national registration scheme was fairly comprehensive. I believe this, despite reports sent to me by officials of my own riding, and despite the very obvious loopholes and short-comings they pointed out to me. Their report to Ottawa was very critical of the whole set-up. I know both the registrar and the deputy registrar, and I know, too, that they did their best, under the circumstances. I have reason to believe that York West was one of the best ridings in Canada so far as national registration was concerned. The deputy registrar, who is a political opponent of mine, is now a census taker for the riding. I may say I have every confidence in him, and I have written and told ffiim so. He pointed out to me, however, several glaring weaknesses in the scheme, which I could not help seeing. Unfortunately I was on duty with my regiment at camp when the registration was undertaken. Since then I have, like all hon. members, heard the rumours as to falsification and dishonest practices. The persistence of them worried me. Eventually the case recently reported to the press concerning registration in Montreal was brought to my attention, so I decided to investigate for myself.
Last Monday, April 28, I arrived in Montreal to see if it were possible to obtain a registration card. Unfortunately I found it only too easy. Representing myself as another person-and I was-I was able to buy a registration card quite easily and openly on St. James street in Montreal. I have it here in my hand. Before I made my purchase I reported to the authorities what I was going to do, and I reported to the authorities after I had made my purchase.

This card, however, should be safeguarded. First, it should be made on special, government banknote non-alterafole paper. Second, each card should be numbered. Third, each card should bear the print of the left index finger on it. Fourth, it should bear a signature. A card of identification such as I have mentioned would

be easily made out and quickly filled in. It would be simple to do. I understand the census-taker is asking over one hundred questions. This identification card could be made out while he was writing the answers on the sheet.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is another small
matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I refer to the tax being imposed upon the moving picture industry. This industry has gone out of its way to cooperate with the government by giving free space and free time. I ask the minister to consider this item of taxation carefully and view it in the light of the tremendous help which this industry has given to Canada.
Another matter is the ten per cent tax on soldiers' railway fares. I protest strongly against this. No words of mine could be strong enough to condemn this additional tax on soldiers' railway fares. This is not the same war that we fought in 1914-18. It probably will be necessary to keep troops in Canada for longer than six months. At the end of six months a soldier is entitled to furlough. Leave is a privilege, but furlough is a right. I urge the government to give these men free transportation on their furloughs. In some military districts the average fare has been worked out at from $10 to $15. On the assumption that we had 100,000 men in Canada, the cost would be between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000. I suggest that this would be money well spent. From the financial point of view, it would be a good investment; from the point of view of morale, I think it is necessary.
I have said that the Canadian people are willing to follow a strong lead. To-day the demand for virile, forceful, dynamic, courageous leadership is growing into a roar-a roar that no man may not heed, a roar that has beheaded one king and dethroned another. This roar may be loud or it may be silent, but if it is there, it must be heeded. The voice of the Canadian people to-day says, "action, action, more action." It is up to us to see that they get it. We in this house are in deadly peril to-day. This very parliament is in. grave danger. The lack of vigour in
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

prosecuting the war is blamed on us. We are the head of the state; like the kings of old, parliament is supreme. This is the theory of
democracy, and I ask each and every hon. member to ask himself if it is working. Are we by our own actions creating confidence in the system we are defending? Are we doing our duty to the country by submitting blindly to government by order in council? Are we mice, or are we men?
I now make a suggestion to the house in all seriousness and sincerity. We must know the conditions with which we expect our men to contend. A good officer will not ask his men to do anything which he is not ready to do himself. We cannot all be in the army, but we can all be in the front line. I suggest that during the recess the government grant an opportunity to all members who so desire to go over to England to act as voluntary air raid precaution workers for a month or so. Nothing would so improve the morale of the Canadian people. Nothing would do more to increase respect for parliament. Nothing would add so greatly to the solidarity of the British empire. Nothing would do more to show the United States that the Canadian people were one hundred per cent in the war. Nothing would do more to show the world that the democracies are tough. Nothing would so effectively stop articles similar to those which have appeared recently in Time and Life. Nothing would so satisfy that one thing which makes us men -our self-respect. Nothing would so show that we are men, not mice.
